After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, the patient shows a major radiologic and biologic response (≈60% volumetric reduction; CEA from 880 to 180 ng/mL). MRI now demonstrates five well-defined residual liver lesions without reported extrahepatic disease. In this context of marked downsizing and clearer lesion delineation, a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant appears potentially achievable. This pattern is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Immediate high-quality restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to reassess precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical conversion strategy
• If imaging confirms feasibility, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of all five lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may be performed as a single-stage or staged hepatectomy.
• The goal is complete clearance of residual disease while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

E. Surveillance
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has eight bilobar metastases, but no detailed information is available on lesion size, exact segmental distribution, relationship to major vascular structures, or calculated future liver remnant (FLR). These data are decisive for determining whether an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate liver function. Because this information is missing, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” At the same time, the disease is not clearly “Not resectable” because conversion to resectability may be possible with further downsizing chemotherapy and/or hypertrophy strategies once the missing anatomic/functional data are obtained.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Molecular work‑up: obtain KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, and MSI status (guides choice of targeted agent).  
• Performance assessment: ECOG, comorbidities, liver function, and baseline hepatic parenchymal quality (steatosis, chemotherapy‑associated injury).  
• Systemic therapy intensification:  
   – If RAS wild‑type, consider FOLFOXIRI + anti‑EGFR (cetuximab or panitumumab).  
   – If RAS‑mutated, use FOLFOXIRI + anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab).  
   – Continue for 2–3 months, aiming for objective response (partial response or ≥30 % reduction in sum of diameters) and CEA decline.  
• Re‑assessment after the intensified regimen: repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
• If imaging shows sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in a non‑injured liver), proceed to surgical planning:  
   – Prefer a liver‑first approach because the primary sigmoid lesion is asymptomatic.  
   – Plan parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections to achieve R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous functional segments.  
   – If FLR is inadequate, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is needed and patient fitness permits).  
   – Aim for a single‑stage or staged hepatectomy that removes all eight lesions; intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult disease.  
• After hepatic resection, reassess the primary tumor: if still resectable and patient remains fit, perform sigmoid resection (laparoscopic low anterior resection) 4–6 weeks later; otherwise, consider endoscopic or radiologic control.  
• Adjuvant chemotherapy: resume peri‑operative systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) post‑hepatectomy, tailored to molecular profile.  
• If after intensification there is radiologic progression or CEA rise, shift to second‑line systemic therapy (e.g., switch irinotecan ↔ oxaliplatin backbone, consider regorafenib or trifluridine/tipiracil) and discuss locoregional ablative options (RFA, SBRT) for residual liver lesions.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
• Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities.  
• Detailed liver imaging: size of each metastasis, exact segmental location, proximity to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary structures.  
• Volumetric liver assessment: total liver volume, tumor burden volume, calculated future liver remnant (percentage and absolute volume).  
• Baseline liver function tests and assessment of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (e.g., steatohepatitis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
• Exact staging of the primary sigmoid tumor (T, N status, margin involvement).  
• Whether the primary tumor has been resected or is planned for resection, and its symptom status.  
• RECIST measurements (baseline and post‑therapy) to quantify response.  
• Patient’s nutritional status and frailty assessment.

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the case lacks critical information that directly determines surgical feasibility, namely a quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and detailed anatomic relationship of the remaining lesions to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures. Until these data are obtained, a definitive decision on upfront resection cannot be made; the patient may become resectable after confirming adequate FLR or after adjunctive measures such as portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a staged approach.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy with the current FOLFOXIRI regimen (or add a biologic agent if molecular profile warrants) to maximise tumour shrinkage; aim for a total of 6–8 cycles unless toxicity limits treatment.  
• Serial monitoring of CEA and repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI with hepatobiliary contrast) after each 2‑cycle block to document response and to identify lesions that have become amenable to resection or ablation.  
• At the time of maximal radiologic response, perform a comprehensive restaging work‑up:  
   – Volumetric liver CT/MRI to calculate FLR (target ≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
   – High‑resolution imaging of the hepatic hilum and major veins to define proximity of residual lesions to portal/hepatic veins and biliary confluence.  
   – Chest CT and pelvic MRI (or endorectal ultrasound) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Assessment of performance status, liver function tests, and chemotherapy‑related liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
• Multidisciplinary decision based on the above data:  
   – If FLR is adequate and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection. For bilobar disease, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if rapid hypertrophy is needed.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolisation (or ligation) to induce hypertrophy, re‑image after 2–4 weeks, and then proceed to resection.  
   – For lesions abutting major vessels where a safe margin cannot be obtained, plan intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided ablation (RFA or microwave) combined with limited resection.  
• Management of the primary rectal tumour:  
   – If the rectal lesion is asymptomatic and down‑staged, a liver‑first approach is preferred; after hepatic surgery, deliver standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (long‑course 5‑FU‑based) followed by low anterior resection.  
   – If the rectal tumour is symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction) or requires urgent treatment, perform resection of the primary first, then resume systemic therapy and reassess hepatic resectability.  
• Post‑operative plan: adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of planned cycles) and consider maintenance biologic therapy based on molecular profile; enrol in surveillance programme with 3‑monthly CEA and 6‑monthly imaging for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver).  
• Exact number, maximal diameter, and segmental distribution of the residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
• Relationship of each lesion to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes).  
• Current status of the primary rectal tumour (local stage, symptoms, need for radiotherapy).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
• Evidence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
• Molecular profile of the tumour (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) to guide targeted therapy.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the two right‑lobe metastases are technically amenable to resection (e.g., right posterior sectionectomy or right hepatectomy with preservation of left liver), but disease progression on first‑line FOLFOX demonstrates aggressive biology and lack of disease control. Current guidelines require disease control with second‑line systemic (or regional) therapy before a curative‑intent liver operation can be offered.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Switch from FOLFOX to a KRAS‑mutant‑appropriate second‑line regimen: FOLFIRI + bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) is the standard choice; consider adding a clinical‑trial option if available.  
- Administer 2–3 cycles of the new regimen, then restage with high‑quality triphasic CT or liver‑specific MRI (including volumetry) to assess tumor response, new lesions, and FLR volume.  
- If imaging shows objective response (≥20 % shrinkage) or at least stable disease with no new extra‑hepatic sites, proceed to surgical planning:  
   • Evaluate future liver remnant; if predicted FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after prior chemotherapy), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy, or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   • Plan a right posterior sectionectomy (segments VII‑VIII) or right hepatectomy, aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous left‑liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   • Decide on timing of primary colon resection: if the primary tumor is still in situ and asymptomatic, a simultaneous colon and liver resection can be performed in a fit 71‑year‑old; if symptomatic or requiring complex reconstruction, stage the procedures (colon first, then liver after recovery).  
- Post‑operative management: resume the same systemic regimen (FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for 4–6 months as adjuvant therapy, provided postoperative recovery is adequate and liver function remains normal.  
- If after second‑line therapy the liver disease remains progressive or new extra‑hepatic sites appear, shift to third‑line options (e.g., regorafenib, trifluridine/tipiracil) or consider liver‑directed locoregional therapies such as Y‑90 radio‑embolisation, hepatic arterial infusion, or percutaneous ablation, recognizing that curative surgery is unlikely.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (resected, unresected, symptomatic, need for stoma).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, cardiopulmonary reserve, and baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume calculation (CT‑based volumetry).  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT/PET‑CT) to rule out occult lung, peritoneal, or nodal disease.  
- Molecular profile beyond KRAS (BRAF, MSI/dMMR) that could influence systemic‑therapy choices.  
- Details of prior chemotherapy tolerance (neuropathy, hematologic toxicity) to guide selection of second‑line regimen.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab the imaging shows complete radiologic disappearance of four liver lesions and reduction of the remaining three. This suggests that a curative‑intent liver operation may be feasible, but two decisive pieces of information are still lacking: (a) precise anatomic location, size and volumetric impact of the residual lesions, and (b) calculated future liver remnant (FLR) with assessment of liver function after chemotherapy‑associated injury. Without these data the surgeon cannot confirm that an R0 resection preserving at least two contiguous functional segments and an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % if chemotherapy‑injured) is possible. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further work‑up.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1. Restaging work‑up  
  • Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to delineate all residual disease, including sites that have radiologically disappeared.  
  • Obtain liver volumetry (CT‑based) to calculate FLR; repeat liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assess for chemotherapy‑related sinusoidal injury.  
  • Confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease with chest CT or PET‑CT.  

- 2. Multidisciplinary review  
  • Present imaging, volumetry and functional data to the MDT (hepatic surgeon, medical oncologist, radiologist, pathologist).  
  • Decide on a single‑stage versus staged hepatic approach based on FLR and lesion distribution.  

- 3. Surgical plan (if FLR adequate)  
  • Proceed to curative‑intent liver resection as soon as possible (ideally within 4–6 weeks after the last chemotherapy cycle) to avoid further tumor progression and additional chemotherapy‑induced liver toxicity.  
  • Include in the resection all sites of initial metastases, even those that have disappeared on imaging, because pathology studies show microscopic persistence in most “disappearing” lesions.  
  • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate occult disease and to guide parenchymal‑sparing resections (segmental or non‑anatomic wedge resections) aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
  • If the primary left‑sided colon tumor has not yet been removed, perform a simultaneous extended left colectomy with primary anastomosis, provided the patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve permits combined surgery.  

- 4. If FLR insufficient  
  • Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, with re‑assessment of FLR after 2–3 weeks.  
  • Alternatively, plan a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if disease distribution allows.  

- 5. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
  • After recovery, resume postoperative chemotherapy with FOLFOX (6 months total peri‑operative chemotherapy) without adding anti‑EGFR agents, as peri‑operative cetuximab/panitumumab has not shown survival benefit and may worsen outcomes in resectable disease.  
  • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact segmental location, size and number of the residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and liver function parameters (bilirubin, INR, platelet count, presence of sinusoidal injury).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. still in situ).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, etc.).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutation status (although panitumumab use implies wild‑type, confirmation is advisable).

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the current imaging shows three residual liver lesions <2 cm after chemotherapy, which suggests technical feasibility, but definitive classification requires (a) a quantitative assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve, and (b) confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum, distant nodes). Without these decisive pieces of information we cannot label the case as “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy to complete an optimal pre‑operative regimen (e.g., 6–8 cycles total). Because the tumour is RAS wild‑type, add an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) to the doublet if not already used, to maximise tumour kill and provide a “proof of time” for tumour biology.  
• Restage after the planned total chemotherapy course:  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to re‑measure each lesion and map segmental location.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <0.5 % body‑weight ratio), plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
• If restaging confirms ≤3 lesions, no extra‑hepatic disease, and adequate FLR, schedule curative‑intent liver surgery:  
   – Perform intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion number and location.  
   – Aim for R0 resection with ≥1 mm microscopic margin; consider parenchymal‑sparing segmental or subsegmental resections.  
   – For lesions abutting major vessels where safe resection would sacrifice too much parenchyma, use adjunctive thermal ablation (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy to achieve complete local control.  
• Address the primary rectal tumour after hepatic clearance (or simultaneously if anatomy and patient condition allow):  
   – If the rectal tumour is still present, give long‑course chemoradiotherapy followed by low anterior resection or abdominoperineal excision, depending on sphincter involvement.  
   – If the primary has already been resected, ensure clear margins and adequate lymphadenectomy.  
• Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy for 3–6 months, preferably the same regimen that achieved response, to eradicate microscopic disease.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; cross‑sectional imaging (MRI or CT) every 6 months for at least 3 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Precise segmental location of the three residual liver lesions and their relationship to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (or functional liver reserve: indocyanine‑green clearance, liver function tests).  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET, peritoneal assessment).  
• Status of the primary rectal tumour (still in situ, symptomatic, prior radiotherapy, need for resection).  
• Patient performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases and has already shown limited progression on FOLFOX (new lesions on recent CT). This progression makes an immediate curative‑intent liver resection unsafe. However, resectability cannot be definitively excluded because critical information needed to judge technical feasibility is missing – specifically the exact number, size and vascular relationship of each hepatic lesion, the calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume, liver function tests, performance status, and molecular profile (RAS/BRAF). These data are decisive for planning a staged or parenchymal‑sparing approach, and for selecting an appropriate conversion chemotherapy regimen. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending those prerequisites.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Molecular work‑up: obtain tumor RAS, BRAF, MSI status (if not already known) to guide targeted therapy.  
• Switch systemic therapy to a more active conversion regimen:  
   – If RAS wild‑type, consider FOLFOXIRI + anti‑EGFR (cetuximab or panitumumab).  
   – If RAS mutant or unknown, consider FOLFIRI + bevacizumab or continue FOLFOX with addition of bevacizumab.  
   – Aim for at least 4–6 cycles (≈2–3 months) with radiologic assessment after every 2 months.  
• Response assessment: repeat high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with volumetric analysis to:  
   – Determine number, size, and distribution of residual lesions.  
   – Calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or <0.5 % body‑weight ratio) plan hypertrophy strategy.  
• If disease is stable or responding and FLR is adequate:  
   – Plan curative‑intent liver surgery. For bilobar disease, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage clears lesions in the future liver remnant, followed by portal vein embolization to induce hypertrophy, then second‑stage major resection).  
   – Alternatively, if FLR is borderline, evaluate portal vein embolization (PVE) or liver venous deprivation (LVD) before the second stage.  
   – For lesions abutting major vessels where parenchymal‑sparing resection would leave <1 cm margins, consider R1 vascular resection or intra‑operative ablation (RFA/MWA) of marginal lesions.  
• Primary tumor management:  
   – If the transverse colon primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or at high risk, perform a colon‑first resection (extended right colectomy) after systemic therapy has achieved disease control.  
   – If the primary is asymptomatic and liver disease is the priority, a liver‑first approach may be chosen, especially if a major hepatectomy is planned.  
   – In selected fit patients without contraindications, simultaneous colon and liver resection can be contemplated only when the liver resection is limited (e.g., non‑major, ≤2 segments).  
• Post‑operative therapy:  
   – Continue peri‑operative FOLFOX‑based chemotherapy for 6 months total (including pre‑operative cycles) as per EORTC 40983 data to improve disease‑free survival.  
   – Consider adjuvant targeted therapy (anti‑EGFR or anti‑VEGF) based on molecular status and prior exposure.  
• If after conversion therapy the disease continues to progress or extra‑hepatic lesions increase, shift to palliative systemic therapy and consider locoregional liver treatments (HAIC, DEB‑TACE, SBRT) for symptom control.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Exact count, maximal diameter, and segmental location of each liver metastasis.  
• Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, indocyanine‑green clearance if available).  
• Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect surgical risk.  
• Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
• Details of the “two new lesions” on the thoraco‑abdominal CT – are they hepatic, pulmonary, or other extra‑hepatic sites?  
• Baseline cardiopulmonary reserve (ejection fraction, pulmonary function) if major thoraco‑abdominal surgery is contemplated.  
• Current CEA trend (baseline vs post‑chemo) to gauge biologic response.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability, select the optimal conversion regimen, and design the surgical plan.

G. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The case contains a decisive missing piece of information: the functional liver reserve (future liver remnant volume) and the anatomic distribution of the seven remaining metastases (unilobar vs bilobar, proximity to major vessels). Without these data a safe R0 resection cannot be confirmed, and the single progressing 5‑cm lesion in segment VII may require down‑staging before surgery. Therefore the patient cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and does not meet criteria for “Not resectable” based on current oncologic or anatomic contraindications.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Confirm primary‑tumor status – if the left‑sided colon primary has not yet been resected, plan either (a) simultaneous colon‑liver resection (if the liver operation will be limited) or (b) staged resection with the liver first (“reverse” approach) because a major hepatectomy is likely required.  
2. Systemic therapy continuation – KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents; continue an oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab) or intensify to FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab if the patient is fit (ECOG 0‑1, adequate marrow, renal and hepatic function).  
3. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months (≈ 6–8 weeks of chemotherapy): repeat triphasic CT/MRI with volumetric analysis.  
   - If all lesions are now ≤ 5 cm, no vascular encasement, and the projected FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % after chemotherapy), proceed to surgical planning.  
   - If the segment VII lesion remains progressive, consider local ablative control (RFA or stereotactic body radiotherapy) to achieve down‑staging.  
4. Pre‑operative liver optimisation – if volumetry shows FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy), perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (resection of lesions in one lobe, PVE, then completion hepatectomy).  
5. Surgical plan – aim for an R0 resection of all viable disease:  
   - Major hepatectomy (right or extended right) to include the segment VII lesion, combined with parenchymal‑sparing resections (non‑anatomical wedge or segmentectomy) for the remaining stable lesions, preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  
   - If any lesion is unresectable due to vascular proximity, treat it with intra‑operative ablation (RFA/ microwave) to achieve negative margins.  
6. Post‑operative management – resume the same systemic regimen (or an adapted one if toxicity occurred) for 3–6 months as adjuvant therapy, unless contraindicated.  
7. Surveillance – CT/MRI every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, with CEA monitoring.

Step 3 – Missing data (essential for a definitive recommendation)  
- Performance status (ECOG/WHO) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and Child‑Pugh score.  
- Detailed imaging of the liver: exact number, size, and segmental location of each of the six stable lesions; relationship to major hepatic veins, portal/hepatic arteries, and biliary structures.  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) before and after chemotherapy.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, or pending resection).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Current chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles already delivered, and response criteria (RECIST) for each lesion.  
- Laboratory tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9) trends.  

These data are required to finalize resectability, choose the optimal systemic regimen, and decide on the need for portal vein embolisation or staged hepatectomy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient shows a radiological complete response after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but current evidence indicates that microscopic residual disease may persist in sites of previously documented metastases. Definitive cure therefore still requires surgical clearance of the original hepatic disease (or at least a confirmatory intra‑operative assessment). Because the decision hinges on a prerequisite surgical action – namely exploration with intra‑operative ultrasound and resection (or ablative treatment) of the prior lesion sites – the case fits the “Potentially resectable” definition. No absolute anatomic or functional contraindication is reported, but essential data needed to confirm technical feasibility are missing.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Confirm disease status before any operation  
   - Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable) to reassess for any occult lesions.  
   - Perform a PET‑CT to evaluate for residual extra‑hepatic disease (especially the lungs).  

2. Assess primary rectal tumor  
   - Review baseline rectal staging (MRI pelvis) and current status (symptoms, response to any neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
   - If the primary remains unresected, plan standard rectal cancer protocol (short‑course radiotherapy or long‑course chemoradiation) followed by curative‑intent low anterior resection (or abdominoperineal resection if required).  

3. Surgical plan for the liver  
   - Schedule a liver‑focused operation with a hepatobiliary surgeon experienced in parenchymal‑sparing techniques.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the original metastatic sites; even if no mass is visible, mark the segmental locations based on pre‑treatment imaging.  
   - Perform limited anatomical resections (segmentectomy/sectionectomy) or non‑anatomical wedge resections of those zones, aiming for R0 margins.  
   - If the future liver remnant (FLR) is estimated <30 % of total liver volume, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy before definitive resection.  
   - In cases where resection would be technically demanding, adjunctive ablative modalities (RFA, microwave ablation, or SBRT) may be employed to achieve complete clearance.  

4. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - After hepatic surgery (and primary resection if applicable), give adjuvant chemotherapy – preferably 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) without biologic agents, as peri‑operative biologics have not shown survival benefit in the resectable setting.  
   - If the primary tumor was not previously irradiated, incorporate the appropriate radiotherapy schedule before or after surgery according to standard rectal cancer guidelines.  

5. Follow‑up  
   - Serial CEA measurements every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Imaging surveillance with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

- Exact number, maximal diameter, and segmental distribution of the original liver metastases.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelets, liver enzymes).  
- Presence, size, and number of any extra‑hepatic lesions (e.g., lung nodules) and their response to chemotherapy.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR status) to guide any targeted adjuvant considerations.  
- Current status of the rectal primary (clinical T/N stage, response to any prior radiotherapy, symptom burden).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.  

These data are essential to finalize the operative plan, confirm that an adequate FLR will remain, and ensure that no residual extra‑hepatic disease precludes a curative approach.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: After 8 cycles of systemic chemotherapy the patient still has three hepatic lesions each larger than 5 cm, indicating a high tumor burden. Current imaging data are insufficient to determine (a) the precise anatomical relationship of the lesions to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures, (b) the volume of the future liver remnant (FLR) that would remain after a curative‑intent resection, and (c) the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., pulmonary or peritoneal metastases). These missing pieces of information are decisive for judging whether an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate hepatic function. Consequently, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and does not meet criteria for “Not resectable” because conversion strategies (additional chemotherapy, portal vein embolization, staged hepatectomy) may render the disease operable once the missing data are clarified.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy with a conversion‑intention regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR agents according to RAS/BRAF status) for an additional 2–4 cycles, aiming for further tumor shrinkage.  
- Re‑image the liver with contrast‑enhanced MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and obtain a volumetric CT scan to:  
   • Define lesion location relative to portal/hepatic veins and biliary ducts.  
   • Calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or <0.5 % liver‑body weight ratio), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the tumor‑bearing lobe.  
- If after the additional chemotherapy the lesions become ≤5 cm and/or reduce in number, reassess for a single‑stage R0 hepatectomy.  
- If FLR remains insufficient after down‑staging, proceed with a two‑stage hepatectomy:  
   1st stage – clearance of metastases in the future liver remnant (ablation or limited resection) combined with PVE of the diseased lobe;  
   2–4 weeks later – repeat imaging to confirm hypertrophy, then perform the definitive major hepatectomy (right or extended right) to remove remaining disease.  
- Consider ALPPS only if rapid hypertrophy is required and the patient’s operative risk is acceptable (ECOG 0‑1, no significant comorbidities).  
- Address the primary colon tumor after hepatic disease control:  
   • If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or at high risk of complications due to T4 invasion, perform a staged colon resection first.  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic, a liver‑first approach is preferred to avoid delaying potentially curative liver surgery.  
- Post‑operative management: adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or tailored based on response) for 3–6 months; consider peri‑operative cetuximab or bevacizumab only if molecular profile supports benefit.  
- Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary review (hepatic surgeon, colorectal surgeon, medical oncologist, radiologist, interventional radiologist) to adjust the plan based on response and emerging data.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed liver imaging (MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and volumetric CT) showing:  
   • Exact number, size, and segmental distribution of each metastasis.  
   • Proximity to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
   • Quantitative future liver remnant volume.  
- Assessment for extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, PET‑CT, diagnostic laparoscopy if indicated).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky), comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve, liver function tests, Child‑Pugh score).  
- Molecular tumor profile of the primary (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) to guide targeted therapy choice.  
- Baseline and post‑chemotherapy RECIST measurements to quantify response.  
- Serum liver function trends (bilirubin, AST/ALT, ALP, INR) to evaluate chemotherapy‑induced hepatotoxicity.  
- Planned surgical margin goals and intra‑operative ultrasound availability.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the residual lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for further systemic therapy.
D. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
E. Previous systemic regimens received and tolerance.
F. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Not resectable  

Reasoning: The patient previously underwent a right hepatectomy, leaving the left liver (segments II, III, IV) as the only functional parenchyma. The current recurrence involves both segments II and III. Resection of these two lesions would require a left‑lateral sectionectomy, which would leave only segment IV (and possibly the caudate lobe) as future liver remnant. This would result in an FLR well below the generally accepted safety threshold of ≥30 % of total liver volume (or ≥0.5 % liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio). Consequently, a curative‑intent hepatectomy is not technically feasible without risking postoperative liver failure. No alternative hypertrophy strategy (e.g., portal vein embolisation) is applicable because the right lobe has already been removed. Therefore the disease is classified as “Not resectable” from a hepatic‑functional standpoint.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic therapy first  
   - Initiate a KRAS‑mutant‑appropriate regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with bevacizumab).  
   - Aim for 3–6 cycles, reassessing radiologically after every 2 cycles.  
   - Monitor CEA trend and liver function tests throughout.  

2. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Perform repeat liver MRI with volumetric analysis to quantify the remaining left‑liver volume and to evaluate tumor response.  
   - If the lesions have responded (size reduction) and the FLR is still inadequate, proceed to step 3.  

3. Locoregional control  
   - Because an anatomic resection would leave insufficient liver, consider parenchyma‑sparing approaches:  
      Percutaneous image‑guided thermal ablation (RFA or microwave) of one or both lesions, aiming for complete necrosis while preserving maximal liver tissue.  
      If lesions are close to major vessels, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) as an alternative.  

4. Multidisciplinary review  
   - Re‑evaluate the patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and liver synthetic function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
   - Discuss the feasibility of a repeat limited hepatectomy (non‑anatomic wedge resections) combined with ablation, only if postoperative FLR can be confirmed ≥30 % after the planned parenchymal‑sparing resection.  

5. Maintenance therapy  
   - After local control (ablation ± limited resection), continue systemic therapy (maintenance bevacizumab ± fluoropyrimidine) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.  

6. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 6 weeks, liver MRI every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months, with chest imaging to rule out pulmonary metastases.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative volumetric measurement of the current left‑liver remnant (FLR) and of the anticipated remnant after a left‑lateral resection.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment of underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.  
- Detailed operative report of the prior right hepatectomy (extent of resection, vascular reconstructions, postoperative complications).  
- Current cross‑sectional imaging of the portal and hepatic veins to confirm patency.  
- Full staging for extra‑hepatic disease (CT chest or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude occult metastases.  
- Information on prior systemic therapy (agents used, response, toxicity) to guide choice of the next chemotherapy regimen.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm) occurring in the left lateral section after a prior right hepatectomy, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesions are peripherally located but arise in the only remaining functional liver. Resection is technically feasible but must strictly preserve adequate parenchyma and inflow/outflow. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy, pending volumetric confirmation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative volumetric and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and ensure preservation of sufficient functional parenchyma.
• Assess portal inflow and venous outflow carefully given prior right hepatectomy.

B. Peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (220 ng/mL) and early recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the 2 lesions of segments II and III aiming for R0 margins.
• Avoid any formal left hepatectomy or extended resection.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of segments II and III on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the first hepatectomy.
E. a chest CT scan F. Exact CEA trend prior to detection of recurrence.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of left R0 hepatectomy for liver metastases three years ago. CEA 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VIII (3.8 cm) in contact with the IVC. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep solitary recurrence, technical assessment of resection required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The solitary 3.8 cm metastasis in segment VIII abuts the IVC, making the technical resection demanding (possible need for vascular control or reconstruction).  
- After a prior left hepatectomy the remaining liver is the right hemiliver; preservation of at least two contiguous segments (e.g., V‑VI) is theoretically possible, but the actual future liver remnant (FLR) volume is unknown.  
- Adequate FLR (≥30 % of total liver volume in a non‑cirrhotic liver) is a decisive criterion; without volumetric data we cannot confirm that the remaining liver will be sufficient, nor can we decide whether portal vein embolization (PVE) is required.  
- Therefore a prerequisite assessment (volumetry/functional liver reserve) must be completed before a definitive “Resectable upfront” decision can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline restaging  
   - Full contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Laboratory panel: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, platelets, albumin; assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1).  
2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (test‑of‑time and biologic selection)  
   - RAS‑wild‑type, therefore a doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) is appropriate.  
   - Administer 2–3 months (≈4–6 cycles), monitor CEA trend and repeat MRI (or CT) to evaluate tumor response and any new lesions.  
3. Re‑assessment of resectability after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Perform volumetric CT/MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), schedule portal vein embolization of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left‑sided remnant (if any viable left‑liver tissue remains) or consider a staged approach.  
   - If imaging shows stable disease or partial response and FLR is adequate, proceed to surgery.  
4. Surgical plan  
   - Goal: R0 resection of the segment VIII lesion with negative margins; aim for ≤1 cm margin (sub‑centimetre margins are acceptable).  
   - Preferred technique: anatomic segment VIII resection or non‑anatomic wedge resection with vascular control of the IVC; if the tumor encircles the IVC, consider IVC tangential resection with primary repair or graft reconstruction, performed by an experienced hepatobiliary team.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
   - Preserve at least two contiguous right‑liver segments (V‑VI) to maintain inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
5. Post‑operative management  
   - Standard enhanced recovery pathway; monitor liver function closely.  
   - Adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen as neoadjuvant, possibly shortened to 3–4 cycles) to treat micrometastatic disease, given the high pre‑operative CEA (180 ng/mL) and prior recurrence.  
   - Serial CEA measurement and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months thereafter.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT/MRI volumetry) and functional liver reserve (e.g., indocyanine‑green clearance, liver stiffness).  
- Comprehensive staging for extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT or PET‑CT).  
- Current status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected, margin status, time since resection).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, cardiopulmonary reserve, and baseline laboratory liver profile.  
- Details of prior hepatic surgery (extent of left hepatectomy, any postoperative complications) that may affect remaining liver quality.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

• Initiate systemic therapy immediately. Preferred regimen: FOLFOX (or FOLFOXIRI if patient fit) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Obtain high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced MRI/CT with volumetry to calculate FLR; aim for >30 % of total liver volume in a chemotherapy‑naïve liver (or >40 % if prior systemic therapy has been given).  
   • Perform liver function assessment (serum bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count, ICG‑R15).  
   • Review performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and confirm that the primary colorectal tumor has been resected or is scheduled for resection.  

2. If FLR is adequate (≥30‑40 % and functional tests acceptable)  
   • Proceed to a single‑stage, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy:  
     – Non‑anatomic wedge resection of the 2.6 cm lesion in segment IVa with a 1‑cm margin.

   • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion borders and vascular structures; apply Pringle maneuver only if necessary and for limited time.  
   • If the segment VIII lesion is adjacent to a major vessel making a safe margin doubtful, perform intra‑operative radiofrequency ablation (RFA) or microwave ablation as an adjunct to achieve complete local control while preserving parenchyma.

   • Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches (or right posterior sector) to induce hypertrophy of the left liver and segment IV. Re‑assess FLR after 2–4 weeks.

5. Post‑operative follow‑up  
   • Monitor CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.

• Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume and proportion of total liver volume.

   – Consider a parenchymal‑sparing, staged approach (first‑stage clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant combined with portal vein embolization of the contralateral lobe to induce hypertrophy).  
   – If FLR remains marginal after PVE, evaluate ALPPS or two‑stage hepatectomy as alternatives, balancing morbidity against potential cure.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound and palpation to confirm complete clearance; aim for R0 resection (margin ≥ 1 mm).  
• For lesions that remain unresectable after maximal systemic therapy, integrate locoregional therapies (percutaneous ablation, selective internal radiation therapy, or hepatic arterial infusion) to achieve local control while continuing systemic treatment.  
• Throughout treatment, monitor CEA and imaging every 8–12 weeks; if extra‑hepatic disease emerges or progression occurs despite therapy, shift to palliative systemic regimen.  

Step 3 – Missing data

• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, albumin, INR) and presence of steatosis or fibrosis.  
• Performance status, comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
• Detailed extra‑hepatic staging (CT chest, PET‑CT if indicated) to exclude lung, peritoneal, or nodal disease.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right hepatectomy in 2021 for three KRAS mutated metastases. Liver MRI 2025: two new lesions segments IVb and II (2.7 and 3.2 cm).No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 300 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar liver recurrence, sufficient liver volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The two new metastases are located in the left liver (segments II and IVb) after a prior right hepatectomy, and the report states that “sufficient liver volume” is present. However, definitive resection requires (a) confirmation that the future liver remnant will remain ≥30 % of total functional liver after removal of the two lesions (precise volumetric analysis) and (b) exclusion of occult extra‑hepatic disease with a PET/CT or equivalent whole‑body staging. In addition, the high CEA (300 ng/mL) and KRAS‑mutated biology argue for a short course of systemic therapy (“proof of time”) before committing to surgery. Until these prerequisites are fulfilled, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Systemic therapy first  
   – Initiate a KRAS‑directed doublet/triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 3–4 cycles.  
   – Monitor CEA after each cycle; aim for a ≥30 % decline or at least a stable trend.  
   – Restage with contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted sequences) and PET/CT to confirm disease control and absence of extra‑hepatic lesions.  

• Pre‑operative assessment  
   – Perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate the future liver remnant after planned resections; ensure FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑induced steatosis is present).  
   – Evaluate liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count) and cardiopulmonary fitness (performance status, comorbidities).  

• Surgical plan (if disease is controlled and FLR adequate)  
   – Aim for a parenchyma‑sparing approach: non‑anatomic wedge resections of segment II and segment IVb with ≥ 1 mm (R1) or preferably ≥ 5 mm margins.  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and detect occult disease.  
   – Preserve at least two contiguous left‑liver segments (II‑III‑IVa) with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   – If FLR is borderline, consider left‑portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches (already resected) to stimulate hypertrophy of the remaining left segments before resection; however, this is rarely needed after a prior right hepatectomy.  

• Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (same regimen or maintenance with fluoropyrimidine + bevacizumab) for 4–6 months as adjuvant therapy, given the high‑risk biology (KRAS‑mutated, elevated CEA).  
   – Serial CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Exact future liver remnant volume (volumetric measurement).  
• Comprehensive liver function tests (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count).  
• Whole‑body PET/CT or equivalent staging to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Current performance status and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected, residual disease, timing of last colorectal surgery).  
• Additional molecular data (BRAF, MSI) that could influence systemic therapy choice.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, history of segmental VI-VII resection. Liver MRI: new lesion segment III (2.4 cm) and micronodule segment II. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous contralateral recurrence, possible minimally invasive approach depending on remnant volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has two left‑lateral lesions (segment III 2.4 cm and a micronodule in segment II) after a prior right‑posterior (VI‑VII) resection.  
- Technically, a left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II + III) would remove all visible disease, but the adequacy of the future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed from the data provided.  
- A definitive decision therefore requires a quantitative FLR assessment (volumetry ± functional test) or, if the FLR is marginal, a pre‑operative maneuver such as portal‑vein embolisation.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Step 2.1 – Complete pre‑operative work‑up  
  • Obtain high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
  • Perform liver function testing (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count) to confirm hepatic reserve.  
  • Restage with whole‑body imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET‑CT) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • Review performance status, comorbidities, and prior chemotherapy exposure.  

- Step 2.2 – Decision based on FLR  
  • If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in a non‑chemotherapy‑injured liver) with adequate inflow/outflow, proceed directly to curative surgery.  
  • If FLR is borderline (20‑30 %), schedule right‑portal‑vein embolisation (PVE) to induce hypertrophy, re‑image after 4‑6 weeks, and then operate.  

- Step 2.3 – Surgical plan  
  • Preferred approach: minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) left‑lateral sectionectomy, aiming for R0 resection with ≥ 1 mm margin (R1 acceptable if postoperative ablation is planned).  
  • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
  • Preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact vascular inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  

- Step 2.4 – Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
  • Given metachronous disease, BRAF wild‑type status and limited tumour burden, adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± biologic) after recovery from surgery is recommended.  
  • Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not mandatory unless FLR is insufficient or there is concern for aggressive biology.  

- Step 2.5 – Post‑operative follow‑up  
  • Serial CEA and imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
  • Consider multidisciplinary review of any new lesions for repeat local therapy (re‑resection, ablation, or systemic treatment).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact size of the segment II micronodule.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and functional reserve (ICG clearance, liver biochemistry).  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile.  
- Evidence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Baseline carcino‑embryonic antigen (CEA) level.  
- Interval since the prior segment VI‑VII resection and any postoperative complications.  
- Details of any prior systemic chemotherapy (agents, cycles, response).  
- Current liver parenchymal quality (steatosis, chemotherapy‑induced injury).  

These items are essential to confirm that a curative, safe hepatic resection is feasible and to tailor the optimal peri‑operative oncologic plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, operated two years earlier with a left hepatectomy.Liver MRI: recurrence segment VIII (3.1 cm) in contact with the middle hepatic vein. CEA 200 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Isolated complex recurrence of the hepatic dome, technical assessment required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The solitary 3.1 cm lesion in segment VIII is technically amenable to a limited resection, but it abuts the middle hepatic vein, raising concern for loss of venous outflow from the remaining right‑lobe segments.  
- After a prior left hepatectomy the future liver remnant (FLR) will consist mainly of the right‑lobe segments V–VII; removal of segment VIII must leave at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow, outflow and biliary drainage.  
- Precise volumetric measurement of the FLR after a segment VIII resection and a detailed assessment of whether the middle hepatic vein can be preserved or reconstructed are essential to confirm technical feasibility.  
- Absence of extra‑hepatic disease has not been documented; this information is also required before declaring the case resectable.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete restaging  
   - Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Laboratory panel: liver function tests, coagulation profile, platelet count, and assessment of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
   - Molecular profiling of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) to guide systemic therapy.  

2. Volumetric and vascular planning  
   - Perform CT‑ or MRI‑based liver volumetry to calculate the FLR after a segment VIII resection; target FLR ≥ 30 % in a liver previously exposed to chemotherapy (≥ 40 % if steatosis/fibrosis is present).  
   - Use high‑resolution imaging (MRI with hepatobiliary contrast or contrast‑enhanced CT) to delineate the extent of middle hepatic vein involvement; discuss with a hepatobiliary vascular surgeon the feasibility of vein preservation, reconstruction, or use of a parenchymal‑sparing “non‑anatomic” resection that spares the vein.  

3. Systemic therapy before definitive surgery  
   - Initiate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to (a) treat occult micrometastatic disease, (b) assess tumor biology (response versus progression), and (c) potentially downsize the lesion if venous involvement is borderline.  
   - Re‑image after chemotherapy to confirm disease stability or response and to re‑evaluate FLR and vascular anatomy.  

4. Surgical approach (if criteria met)  
   - Proceed to a repeat, parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment VIII with negative (R0) margins.  
   - Preserve the middle hepatic vein if possible; if resection of a portion of the vein is unavoidable, plan for venous reconstruction (e.g., autologous graft or prosthetic conduit) or consider a limited “central” resection that includes the vein with reconstruction while maintaining outflow from segments V and VII.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and to detect any additional occult metastases.  

5. Alternative local therapy  
   - If FLR is insufficient or venous reconstruction is deemed unsafe, treat the lesion with percutaneous ablative therapy (RFA or microwave) combined with systemic chemotherapy.  

6. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑month adjuvant FOLFOX) after recovery, guided by postoperative CEA trend and pathology (margin status, tumor regression grade).  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3–4 months for the first two years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume after a planned segment VIII resection.  
- Detailed hepatic venous anatomy: exact length of middle hepatic vein involvement and feasibility of preservation or reconstruction.  
- Evidence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET, peritoneal/lymph node assessment).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities.  
- Prior systemic therapy regimen, response, and interval since last chemotherapy.  
- Molecular profile of the primary colorectal cancer (RAS, BRAF, MSI).

Case_Content:
Man, 72 years old, right hepatectomy 4 years ago. Current liver MRI: multiple nodules segment III, 1-2 cm. CEA 550 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Multifocal recurrence, assessment of resectability and local alternatives.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Not resectable  

Reasoning:  
- The patient has already undergone a right hepatectomy, leaving only the left liver (segments II, III, IV).  
- Current MRI shows multiple 1–2 cm metastases confined to segment III. Resection of all visible disease would require removal of the entire left‑lateral sector (segments II + III) or at least a non‑anatomic resection of segment III that would leave only segment IV.  
- Technical criteria for curative resection demand preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow, outflow and biliary drainage. After removal of segment III, the remaining segments (II and IV) are not contiguous, violating this requirement.  
- Even a limited left‑lateral sectorectomy would leave a future liver remnant (FLR) of < 20 % of total liver volume in a 72‑year‑old, which is below the safety threshold for patients with prior major hepatic surgery.  
- No data are provided on FLR volumetry, liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, Child‑Pugh), or extra‑hepatic disease; however, based on anatomy alone the current intra‑hepatic disease cannot be removed while satisfying the core technical criteria. Hence the case is deemed surgically unresectable at this time.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Initiate a first‑line regimen appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease, e.g., FOLFOX + cetuximab (or FOLFIRI + cetuximab if oxaliplatin‑intolerant).  
   - Treat for 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles), reassessing response with RECIST and, importantly, with morphologic criteria on MRI (to gauge tumor biology).  

2. Restaging after conversion therapy  
   - Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
   - Perform chest CT/PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Re‑measure CEA; a falling trend supports favorable biology.  

3. Decision point after restaging  
   - If lesions shrink sufficiently (e.g., become solitary or limited to a single small focus) and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % with normal liver function), re‑evaluate for a parenchyma‑sparing non‑anatomic wedge resection of the remaining lesion(s) in segment III, preserving segments II + IV as contiguous remnant.  
   - If FLR remains inadequate but disease is controlled, consider local ablative therapy (percutaneous microwave or radiofrequency ablation) of the segment III nodules, which can achieve local control without further loss of liver parenchyma.  

4. Adjunctive liver‑targeted approaches (if needed)  
   - Portal vein embolization (PVE) is not feasible because the right portal branches are already resected; however, associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) is contraindicated given the limited residual liver.  
   - Therefore, the primary liver‑directed option after systemic therapy is percutaneous ablation.  

5. Post‑local therapy systemic management  
   - Continue maintenance chemotherapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine + anti‑EGFR) for 3–6 months after local control, aiming to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3 months for the first year.  

6. Consideration of primary colorectal tumor  
   - If the primary tumor has not been resected, schedule curative‑intent colorectal resection (segmental colectomy or low anterior resection) after systemic therapy and once hepatic disease is controlled, preferably in a staged fashion to avoid simultaneous major hepatectomy.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant (CT or MRI‑based).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh score).  
- Performance status / comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve, ASA classification).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on chest CT or PET‑CT.  
- Details of prior systemic therapy (agents used, response, cumulative oxaliplatin exposure).  
- Time interval since the previous right hepatectomy and any postoperative complications that might affect liver regeneration.  
- Molecular profile beyond RAS (e.g., BRAF, MSI status) that could influence systemic therapy choice.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple metachronous nodules (1–2 cm) in segment III after a prior right hepatectomy, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although confined to the left lateral section, the multifocal pattern in the only remaining liver raises concern for achieving complete clearance while preserving adequate functional parenchyma. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior major hepatectomy, this situation is considered potentially unresectable, but requires careful balance between parenchymal preservation and oncologic completeness.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define the exact number, distribution, and vascular/biliary relationships of the nodules.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

– Parenchymal-sparing wedge/limited resections for accessible lesions.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

A. Exact number and precise segmental distribution of nodules within segment III.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the lesions.
