Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The case is technically feasible (five bilobar lesions, all ≤3.5 cm, and only contact with the middle hepatic vein), but decisive information is missing: an accurate future liver remnant (FLR) volumetric assessment and overall hepatic functional reserve. Without confirming that a ≥20‑30 % FLR (or >0.5 % body weight) can be preserved, the surgery cannot be scheduled outright. Therefore the disease is classified as potentially resectable pending FLR evaluation (and, if needed, portal vein embolisation or a staged approach).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy: Begin 3–4 months of modern doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with bevacizumab, because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective) and the CEA is markedly elevated, indicating aggressive biology.  
- Restaging after induction: Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and calculate FLR volume. Assess response of all liver lesions and look for any new extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum).  
- Decision point:  
   • If FLR ≥30 % of total liver volume and all lesions remain resectable with clear margins, proceed to definitive liver surgery.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolisation (PVE) of the lobe to be resected, re‑image after 2–3 weeks to confirm hypertrophy, then proceed to liver resection.  
   • If disease progression occurs (>3 new lesions or growth of >2 lesions), consider changing systemic regimen (e.g., switch to FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) and reassess after another 2 months.  
- Surgical plan: Aim for an R0, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy. Options include:  
   • One‑stage combined right‑plus‑left‑sided non‑anatomic resections (or segmental resections) to clear all five lesions while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
   • If the middle hepatic vein involvement precludes a safe margin, consider a limited venous reconstruction or a staged approach (right hepatectomy first, then left‑sided resections after hypertrophy).  
- Primary tumour: If the primary colon tumour has not yet been resected, schedule a simultaneous colectomy (preferably laparoscopic left‑sided resection) during the liver operation if the patient’s physiologic reserve permits; otherwise, perform colon resection 4–6 weeks after hepatic surgery once recovery is adequate.  
- Adjuvant therapy: Resume postoperative systemic chemotherapy (same regimen as induction, possibly shortened to 3 months) to address micrometastatic disease, given the high pre‑operative CEA and KRAS mutation.  
- Surveillance: Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (Charlson index).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury.  
- Precise future liver remnant volume calculation from imaging.  
- Status of the primary colon tumour (resected vs. pending).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Details of vascular involvement beyond simple contact (e.g., encasement, invasion) of the middle hepatic vein.  
- Patient’s nutritional status and cardiopulmonary fitness for major hepatectomy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is potentially resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the three lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. a chest CT scan
E. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has seven liver metastases (2‑5 cm) distributed bilaterally, which technically could be removed if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved, possibly after portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a staged hepatectomy. However, two decisive pieces of information are missing – (a) quantitative assessment of FLR and overall liver function, and (b) the patient’s performance status/comorbidities that determine surgical fitness. Moreover, the aggressive biology (BRAF V600E, CEA 1600 ng/mL, synchronous disease) warrants a trial of systemic therapy first to test disease control (“proof of time”). Therefore the case meets the definition of “potentially resectable” because a specific prerequisite (neoadjuvant systemic therapy and FLR assessment) must be completed before definitive surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic therapy immediately:  
   – Preferred regimen for BRAF‑mutated mCRC is a triplet (FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab, or the BEACON‑compatible regimen (encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib) after an induction phase.  
   – Plan 2–3 months of therapy, then restage with high‑quality multiphase CT or MRI (including liver‑specific contrast) to evaluate tumor response, lesion size, and to calculate FLR.  

• If disease is stable or responding (no new lesions, ≤20 % growth of existing lesions):  
   – Re‑assess technical resectability.  
   – If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, schedule portal vein embolisation (PVE) to induce hypertrophy, or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (resection of lesions in one lobe, PVE, then second‑stage clearance).  
   – For lesions in locations unsuitable for resection, plan adjunctive local therapies (radiofrequency ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy) to achieve an R0‑equivalent clearance.  

• Surgical sequence (liver‑first approach):  
   1. Perform liver‑directed surgery once an adequate FLR is confirmed and disease control is demonstrated. Aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions, using anatomical or non‑anatomical resections as dictated by lesion distribution.  
   2. After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), proceed with definitive resection of the primary right colon tumour (right hemicolectomy) with standard oncologic lymphadenectomy.  

• Post‑operative management:  
   – Resume systemic therapy (same regimen or maintenance bevacizumab) for at least 6 months as adjuvant treatment, adjusting based on postoperative recovery and tolerability.  
   – Monitor CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   – Consider enrolment in a clinical trial targeting BRAF‑mutated mCRC or investigating peri‑operative immunotherapy, given the high‑risk molecular profile.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
Essential information not provided that is required for a definitive plan:  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary, hepatic, renal).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and quantitative future liver remnant volume.  
- Precise anatomical distribution of the seven metastases (segmental location, proximity to major vessels/ducts).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on full staging (CT chest, PET‑CT if available).  
- Patient’s nutritional status and body habitus (which influence FLR calculations).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy versus palliative intent.

The patient presents with seven liver metastases (2–5 cm) in the setting of a right T4aN2 colon cancer and a BRAF V600E mutation with very high CEA (1600 ng/mL). Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has four bilobar liver metastases and a locally advanced upper rectal cancer (T3N2). Technical resectability cannot be confirmed without detailed liver volumetry, lesion size and location, and assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR). Moreover, the rectal primary requires neoadjuvant therapy (radiotherapy ± chemoradiation) before safe resection, and the MSI‑H status makes first‑line immune checkpoint inhibition the preferred systemic approach. Therefore resection cannot be performed upfront; it will depend on (a) response to initial immunotherapy and (b) confirmation that an adequate FLR can be preserved (or that portal vein embolisation/ staged hepatectomy can be employed).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate first‑line immunotherapy for MSI‑H metastatic disease (e.g., pembrolizumab 200 mg q3 weeks or nivolumab + ipilimumab per guideline).  
• Baseline high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and volumetric analysis to define FLR and map each metastasis.  
• Re‑stage after 2–3 months of immunotherapy (CT/MRI). Assess:  
    – Radiologic response of liver lesions (RECIST).  
    – Change in CEA (target < 200 ng/mL as a response indicator).  
    – FLR volume; if FLR < 30 % (or <0.5 % body‑weight), plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
• If liver disease becomes technically resectable and no new extra‑hepatic sites appear, schedule hepatic surgery first (liver‑first strategy) because the rectal primary is still locally advanced and will need radiotherapy.  
    – Perform parenchymal‑sparing resections (non‑anatomic or segmental) aiming for R0 margins, preserving ≥2 contiguous segments of liver.  
    – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions.  
    – If FLR remains marginal after first‑stage resection, complete PVE‑induced hypertrophy then proceed with second‑stage hepatectomy.  
• After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈4–6 weeks), deliver neoadjuvant radiotherapy for the rectal tumour:  
    – Short‑course (5 × 5 Gy) followed by a 6‑week interval, or long‑course chemoradiation (50.4 Gy with capecitabine) if tumour‑related risk factors (e.g., threatened mesorectal fascia) are present.  
• Perform definitive rectal surgery (low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, or abdominoperineal resection if sphincter cannot be preserved). Create a diverting stoma if indicated.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy may be considered (e.g., continuation of immunotherapy for a total of 2 years, or switch to a fluoropyrimidine‑based regimen if disease progresses).  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and pelvic MRI every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Precise size (maximum diameter) and segmental location of each liver metastasis.  
• Volumetric assessment of total liver volume and future liver remnant (FLR).  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelets, ICG clearance if available).  
• Performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
• Detailed pelvic MRI staging (mesorectal fascia involvement, distance to sphincter, nodal stations).  
• Presence or absence of other extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
• Patient preference regarding sphincter preservation and willingness for staged procedures.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, two liver metastases segments II and III (3.2 and 4.0 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 320 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 positive.
MDT Discussion: Limited involvement but HER2 mutation may influence systemic therapeutic strategy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Two liver metastases are confined to segments II and III (3.2 cm and 4.0 cm). A left‑lateral sectionectomy would remove both lesions while preserving the right liver, which in most adults provides >30 % future liver remnant (FLR).  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported on the abdominal CT, but a complete staging work‑up (chest CT/PET, pelvic MRI) has not been documented.  
- Critical information required to confirm technical feasibility is missing: quantitative FLR volume, liver function tests, and the patient’s performance status/comorbidities. Without these data the surgeon cannot guarantee safe postoperative liver function. Hence the case is “potentially resectable” pending confirmation of adequate FLR and fitness for surgery.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging and fitness assessment  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT volumetry) to calculate FLR.  
   - Perform chest CT or PET‑CT to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Record ECOG/ASA status, cardiac and pulmonary evaluation, and baseline liver biochemistry (bilirubin, INR, AST/ALT, albumin).  

2. Multimodal treatment sequencing (preferred option)  
   - Neoadjuvant phase (optional but advisable given synchronous disease, N1 nodal status and markedly elevated CEA).  
     • 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with HER2‑directed therapy (trastuzumab + pertuzumab, or trastuzumab‑deruxtecan if available).  
     • Re‑image after chemotherapy to confirm response and verify FLR remains adequate.  
   - Surgical phase – If FLR ≥ 30 % and no extra‑hepatic disease:  
     • Perform a simultaneous curative‑intent operation: left‑sided colectomy (segmental or extended left hemicolectomy) together with left‑lateral liver resection (segments II‑III).  
     • Intra‑operative ultrasound to rule out occult lesions and achieve R0 margins (>1 mm).  
   - Adjuvant phase – Post‑operative systemic therapy for 6 months:  
     • Continue HER2‑targeted therapy (trastuzumab ± pertuzumab) together with standard adjuvant FOLFOX.  
     • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

3. Alternative strategy (if FLR insufficient or comorbidities preclude simultaneous surgery)  
   - Stage the procedures: first liver resection (left‑lateral sectionectomy) after portal vein embolization if FLR < 30 %; then, after recovery, address the primary colon tumor.  
   - Follow the same peri‑operative systemic regimen as above.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- ECOG/ASA performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiac, pulmonary, renal).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, transaminases, albumin) and assessment of underlying liver disease.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT or MRI volumetry).  
- Full extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT or PET‑CT, peritoneal assessment).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status (relevant for anti‑EGFR exclusion, though HER2 positivity already guides therapy).  
- MSI/dMMR status (impacts eligibility for immunotherapy in the peri‑operative setting).

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The right portal pedicle is infiltrated and nine bilobar lesions are present, which presently precludes an R0 resection while preserving two contiguous liver segments and adequate inflow/outflow. Conversion to resectability will require a specific prerequisite: neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (to down‑size disease and test tumor biology) followed by a hypertrophy‑inducing maneuver such as portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage/ALPPS strategy to obtain a sufficient future liver remnant (FLR). Until these steps are completed the disease is not technically resectable.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy  
  • Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR excluded).  
  • Duration: 2–3 months, then restaging with triphasic CT or MRI and CEA.  
- Response assessment  
  • Goal: ≥30 % reduction of total tumor volume, no new lesions, and stable extra‑hepatic sites.  
  • If progression occurs, switch to second‑line (e.g., FOLFIRI + anti‑VEGF) or consider enrolment in a clinical trial.  
- Conversion to resectability (if response achieved)  
  1. Portal vein embolisation of the right portal branch to hypertrophy the left liver (target FLR ≥ 30 % in a healthy liver).  
  2. Re‑imaging 4–6 weeks post‑PVE to confirm adequate FLR and reassess residual disease.  
  3. Surgical plan – most likely a staged approach:  
     - Stage 1: Resection/ablation of left‑lobe lesions (or left hepatectomy) after PVE, preserving left segments as FLR.  
     - Stage 2 (4–8 weeks later): Right hepatectomy with portal pedicle resection and reconstruction if needed, aiming for R0 margins.  
  4. Alternative – If FLR hypertrophy is insufficient or disease remains extensive, consider ALPPS (associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy) provided the patient’s performance status permits.  
- Primary colon tumour  
  • Perform a “liver‑first” strategy: address hepatic disease first, then resect the primary colon tumour (right hemicolectomy with en‑bloc mesocolic excision) once hepatic clearance is achieved and the patient has recovered from liver surgery.  
  • If the primary tumour becomes symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) before hepatic clearance, intervene with diverting stoma or urgent resection.  
- Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
  • Post‑operative systemic therapy (same regimen or adapted) for at least 6 months, tailored to pathological response and residual risk factors (T4, N2, KRAS‑mutated).  
- Surveillance  
  • CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and chest CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelet count, ICG clearance).  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Presence, number and size of extra‑hepatic metastases (e.g., pulmonary nodules) on high‑resolution chest CT or PET‑CT.  
- Molecular profile beyond KRAS (BRAF status, MSI/MMR).  
- Exact extent of portal pedicle invasion (length of involvement, feasibility of vascular reconstruction).  
- Baseline nutritional status and frailty assessment.  
- Patient’s preference regarding aggressive staged surgery versus palliative intent.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with nine bilobar liver metastases associated with infiltration of the right portal pedicle and a very high CEA (2500 ng/mL) in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer. The combination of extensive bilobar disease and portal pedicle involvement precludes the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2500 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response and reassess vascular relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate venous outflow preservation or need for reconstruction.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major response occurs with regression of portal pedicle involvement and significant reduction in tumor burden.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective and dependent on restoration of clear vascular anatomy.

E. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains extensive, consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact extent of portal pedicle infiltration on MRI.
B. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
C. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for intensive systemic therapy.
D. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
E. Liver function assessment in case future conversion is considered. 
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 61 years old, T3N1M1 rectal tumor, three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII). CEA 680 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: extension to the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Metastases near venous confluence, high surgical risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The three metastases are technically resectable only after addressing two decisive issues: (a) the proximity to the hepatic‑vein confluence makes an R0 resection hazardous without either tumor downsizing or vascular reconstruction; (b) the future liver remnant (FLR) has not been quantified, and a major right‑sided resection (segments VI + VIII + IVa) will likely leave a marginal FLR.  
- Consequently, neoadjuvant systemic therapy (to assess tumor biology and possibly shrink the lesions) and a volumetric FLR assessment (with portal‑vein embolisation if needed) are prerequisite actions before a safe curative hepatectomy can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy: 2–3 months of intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) given the KRAS‑mutated, BRAF‑wild‑type biology and the high CEA level. Aim to obtain radiologic response and “proof of time” for disease control.  
- Restaging after induction: repeat triphasic CT/MRI with volumetric analysis of the FLR; assess response of each lesion, especially the one abutting the hepatic‑vein confluence. If FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy), schedule right‑portal vein embolisation (PVE) and re‑image in 2–3 weeks.  
- Surgical sequencing (liver‑first approach):  
   Perform a right hepatectomy extended to segment IVa (right trisectionectomy) with en‑bloc removal of the lesion at the hepatic‑vein confluence; if necessary, reconstruct the involved hepatic vein using a patch or interposition graft to preserve outflow.  
   Aim for R0 margins (≥1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
- Rectal primary management: after hepatic recovery (≈4–6 weeks), deliver neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the T3 N1 rectal tumor (if not already given) followed by total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection according to sphincter involvement).  
- Adjuvant therapy: complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic therapy (including the induction regimen) and consider postoperative oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy ± anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) if the tumor remains KRAS‑mutated (note that anti‑EGFR is ineffective in KRAS‑mutated disease; thus continue bevacizumab‑containing regimen).  
- Surveillance: serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance (to gauge hepatic reserve).  
- Precise maximal diameter of each liver lesion and exact relationship to the right, middle, and left hepatic veins.  
- Quantified future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung nodules, peritoneal implants).  
- Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and whether it is causing obstructive or bleeding symptoms.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding staged versus simultaneous surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII) with MRI showing extension toward the hepatic vein confluence. Although the number of lesions is limited, their proximity to the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely tumor downsizing.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (680 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA (680 ng/mL), KRAS mutation, and complex vascular location, initiate 3–6 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Expert vascular restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate venous outflow preservation or need for reconstruction.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If sufficient tumor regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections, or standard anatomic major hepatectomy with or without vascular reconstruction aiming for R0 margins.

E. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise relationship of each lesion to the hepatic vein confluence on MRI.
B. Liver function assessment in case future conversion is considered. 
C. Feasibility of venous preservation versus reconstruction.
D. Detailed pelvic MRI for rectal treatment planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. chest CT scan
G. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of four bilobar metastases does not preclude resection if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved. However, a segment VII lesion invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over 1 cm, which requires complex vascular reconstruction and is only feasible in highly selected patients. Critical information needed to determine technical feasibility—specifically the calculated FLR volume and the exact circumferential extent of IVC involvement—is not provided. Therefore the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and, because a concrete prerequisite (FLR assessment and possible IVC reconstruction planning) is required, it is “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological and surgical sequence  
• Initiate systemic therapy with an intensive doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status, aiming for tumor down‑staging and biological assessment; repeat CEA and imaging after 2–3 cycles.  
• Perform a comprehensive restaging work‑up: contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including vascular phase) to re‑measure IVC involvement, volumetric CT to calculate FLR, chest CT/PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease, and full liver function panel (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available).  
• If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or an ALPPS procedure to induce hypertrophy before definitive hepatic resection.  
• Re‑evaluate response: if disease is stable or responding and IVC invasion is limited to a segmental wall (<2 cm longitudinally, non‑circumferential), schedule a liver‑first approach with en‑bloc hepatic resection of the involved segments (including segment VII) and segmental IVC resection/reconstruction using a prosthetic or autologous graft, in collaboration with a vascular/thoracic surgeon.  
• Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow; aim for R0 margins (>1 mm). Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm complete clearance.  
• After hepatic surgery and recovery, address the primary left‑sided colon tumor. If the primary is asymptomatic and patient’s condition permits, perform a simultaneous colectomy (laparoscopic or open) during the same anesthesia; otherwise, schedule a staged colectomy within 4–6 weeks.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or modified based on tolerance) for a total of 6 months, with serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3–4 months for the first two years.  
• Consider enrollment in a clinical trial or use of peri‑operative targeted therapy (e.g., anti‑VEGF) if disease biology suggests high recurrence risk.

• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver).  
• Detailed description of IVC invasion (length, circumferential involvement, proximity to hepatic veins).  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
• Cardiopulmonary reserve and performance status (ASA, ECOG).  
• Staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, N‑stage, presence of mesenteric nodal disease).  
• Chest imaging results to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
• Presence or absence of other extra‑hepatic disease (peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
• Patient’s preferences and psychosocial factors influencing aggressive multimodal therapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, five liver metastases including one 8.5 cm in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 870 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis with bilateral portal contact, complex technical discussion.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has five bilobar metastases, including an 8.5 cm central lesion in segment IVb with bilateral portal vein contact, indicating that a major hepatectomy (likely extended right or right + segment IV) would be required. Whether an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be judged from the data provided. Critical missing information includes quantitative FLR volume, baseline liver function, and overall performance status. Moreover, down‑staging with systemic chemotherapy (and possibly portal vein embolization) is typically needed to improve the chance of a safe, curative resection in this setting. Hence the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category because a specific prerequisite (pre‑operative chemotherapy ± PVE and FLR assessment) must be completed before surgery can be planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately: preferred regimen FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
• After 2–3 months (≈ 6 cycles), restage with high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and repeat volumetric analysis to determine FLR percentage and assess tumor response (RECIST).  
• If disease is stable or responding and FLR ≥30 % (or liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio > 0.5) → proceed to definitive liver surgery.  
  – Plan a single‑stage extended right hepatectomy (including segment IV) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm clearance of all lesions; use parenchymal‑sparing techniques or adjunctive radiofrequency ablation for lesions abutting major vessels where safe margins are doubtful.  
  – Perform R0 resection with ≥1 mm microscopic margin; preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
• If FLR is insufficient after chemotherapy (e.g., <30 %):  
  – Perform right‑portal vein embolization (or left‑PVE if left lobe will be the remnant) to induce hypertrophy; re‑image in 2–4 weeks.  
  – If hypertrophy achieves adequate FLR, proceed with the same hepatectomy as above.  
  – If FLR remains inadequate or disease remains extensive, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future remnant lobe plus PVE; second stage: resection of the diseased lobe) or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is required and patient fitness permits.  
• Primary colon tumor management:  
  – Because the primary is right‑sided T4N2, a “liver‑first” approach is advisable after the liver resection, provided the patient recovers without complications.  
  – If the primary becomes symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) during chemotherapy, address it surgically before or concurrently with liver surgery, depending on operative risk.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months, considering addition of anti‑VEGF continuation if tolerated.  
• Surveillance: CEA, CT/MRI of chest/abdomen every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT‑based volumetry).  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and presence of steatosis or fibrosis.  
• Patient performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Confirmation of absence or presence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on staging PET‑CT or chest CT.  
• Molecular profile beyond KRAS (e.g., BRAF, MSI status) that may influence systemic therapy choice.  
• Detailed vascular anatomy of the central lesion (extent of portal/hepatic artery involvement) to plan possible vascular reconstruction.  
• Response to initial chemotherapy (if already started) and any chemotherapy‑induced liver injury.

Case_Content:
Man, 73 years old, transverse colon tumor, two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 70 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Normal CEA despite high volume, question regarding biological sensitivity for follow-up.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient has two liver metastases measuring 4.2 cm and 4.8 cm, which are within the size range that can be resected provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved. However, critical information required to determine technical feasibility is missing:  

- Precise anatomic location of each lesion (unilobar vs. bilobar, relation to major vessels and biliary structures)  
- Volumetric liver assessment (MRI‑based FLR calculation)  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets, AST/ALT) and assessment of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury  
- Performance status (ECOG), comorbidity burden (Charlson index) and cardiopulmonary fitness for major hepatectomy  
- Staging of the primary transverse colon cancer (T‑stage, nodal status) and presence of any extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, PET‑CT)  

Because these data are decisive for surgical planning, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The missing information defines a prerequisite step (comprehensive imaging and functional assessment) before a definitive surgical decision, fitting the definition of “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  

1. Initial systemic therapy  
   - Start a doublet chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS/BRAF wild‑type status.  
   - Aim for 2–3 months (≈6–8 cycles) to assess tumor biology (“proof of time”) and achieve possible downsizing of liver lesions.  

2. Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Perform high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) for precise lesion mapping and FLR volumetry.  
   - Obtain a chest CT and, if available, FDG‑PET/CT to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Repeat CEA measurement; a decline below 80 ng/mL supports favorable biology.  

3. Multidisciplinary re‑assessment  
   - If imaging shows stable or responding disease with no new lesions and an FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % body weight), proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   - If lesions remain borderline (e.g., bilobar distribution with insufficient FLR), consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to augment FLR.  

4. Surgical plan  
   - Primary tumor: Standard oncologic transverse colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy and clear circumferential margins (≥1 mm).  
   - Liver metastases:  
      If both lesions are in the same hepatic lobe and adequate margin can be obtained, perform a single‑stage anatomical or non‑anatomical resection (segmentectomy or wedge) preserving at least two contiguous segments.  
      If lesions are bilobar or FLR is marginal, schedule a staged approach (e.g., right hepatectomy first, followed by left‑lobe resection after hypertrophy) or combine resection with ablative modalities (RFA/SBRT) for lesions in difficult locations.  
   - Aim for R0 resection of all disease.  

5. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Continue the same chemotherapy regimen for 2–3 cycles post‑operatively (adjuvant) if the pathological risk score (e.g., >2 CRS factors) suggests high recurrence risk.  
   - Consider postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (Charlson index)  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, AST/ALT, platelet count) and assessment for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury  
- Precise hepatic lesion locations relative to vascular and biliary structures  
- Volumetric liver imaging (MRI with FLR calculation)  
- Chest imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases  
- Full staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, N‑stage) and any local invasion  
- Nutritional status (weight, albumin) and cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., cardiopulmonary exercise testing)  
- Planned surgical margins for the colon resection (ensuring ≥1 mm)  

These data are essential to confirm technical resectability, assess operative risk, and finalize the optimal treatment sequence.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, left T4N1M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 1400 ng/mL. KRAS G12C mutation confirmed.
MDT Discussion: Specific molecular profile, may benefit from a later targeted strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient has six liver metastases (largest 5.6 cm) arising from a T4N1 left‑sided colon cancer with a KRAS G12C mutation and a markedly elevated CEA (1400 ng/mL). Current imaging confirms the number and size of lesions but does not provide critical information required to determine technical feasibility, namely:  

- Bilobar versus unilateral distribution of the metastases  
- Proximity to major vascular or biliary structures (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery, hepatic ducts)  
- Predicted future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve (e.g., CT volumetry, indocyanine‑green clearance)  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) beyond the liver  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and hepatic function (bilirubin, albumin, portal hypertension)  

Without these data a definitive “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable” judgment cannot be made; however, the disease burden is within the range that can be converted to resection after appropriate down‑staging and/or liver‑volume augmentation, justifying the “Potentially resectable” label.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Initial systemic therapy (conversion intent)  
   - Start a doublet or triplet chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑VEGF antibody (bevacizumab), because KRAS G12C predicts lack of response to anti‑EGFR agents.  
   - Consider adding a KRAS G12C‑specific inhibitor (e.g., sotorasib or adagrasib) within a clinical trial or compassionate‑use program after the standard backbone chemotherapy, as emerging data suggest activity in KRAS‑mutant mCRC.  

2. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months (≈6 cycles)  
   - Repeat high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with liver‑specific contrast and obtain volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
   - Evaluate radiologic response (RECIST) and biological response (CEA trend).  
   - Confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic lesions.  

3. Decision points based on re‑assessment  
   - If sufficient FLR (≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % if steatosis/chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and all lesions become resectable with clear margins: proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   - If FLR is insufficient but disease is responding: schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, followed by re‑evaluation in 4–6 weeks.  
   - If disease remains extensive or progresses: continue systemic therapy (switch to second‑line regimen, e.g., FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) and consider liver‑directed locoregional therapies (Y‑90 radioembolisation, hepatic arterial infusion, or stereotactic body radiotherapy) as bridge to possible later resection.  

4. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - Because the primary is left‑sided T4N1 but the patient is currently asymptomatic, defer definitive colorectal resection until after systemic therapy unless obstructive symptoms develop.  
   - If the primary becomes symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) during chemotherapy, perform a staged colectomy (either before or after liver surgery depending on operative risk and timing).  

5. Post‑operative (adjuvant) strategy  
   - After an R0 liver resection (and primary resection if performed), resume the same systemic regimen for 3–6 months as adjuvant therapy, adjusting for tolerance and residual disease.  
   - Continue KRAS G12C‑targeted therapy if the patient is enrolled in a trial or if the drug is approved for maintenance in this setting.  

6. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA measurements every 6–8 weeks during treatment and every 3 months after surgery.  
   - Imaging (CT or MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

- Detailed liver imaging: bilobar vs. unilateral distribution, relationship to major vessels/ducts, and volumetric assessment for future liver remnant.  
- Confirmation of extra‑hepatic disease status (e.g., chest CT, PET‑CT, peritoneal assessment).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidity burden (Charlson index), and baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, indocyanine‑green clearance).  
- Planned timing and feasibility of primary tumor resection (symptomatic vs. asymptomatic).  
- Availability of KRAS G12C‑targeted therapy (clinical trial enrollment or approved use).  

These data are essential to finalize resectability classification and to tailor the precise surgical and systemic treatment plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, low T3N2M1 rectal cancer, four peripheral liver metastases (2-3.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 90 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS, positive circulating tumor cells.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating cells despite low volume, prognostic significance discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The four peripheral liver metastases (2‑3.5 cm) appear technically amenable to R0 resection with preservation of ≥30 % future liver remnant, and no vascular or biliary invasion is reported. However, unfavorable oncologic features (synchronous presentation, N2 nodal disease, elevated CEA 90 ng/mL, and circulating tumor cells) argue for a “proof of time” approach. Therefore a prerequisite systemic‑therapy phase is required before definitive hepatic surgery can be deemed appropriate.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate conversion systemic therapy: 6 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type and rectal in origin.  
• Restaging after chemotherapy (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI + pelvic MRI, plus repeat CT chest) to:  
   – Confirm that all liver lesions remain resectable and assess tumor response (RECIST).  
   – Verify absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Perform volumetric analysis to calculate future liver remnant; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolization or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
• If restaging confirms resectability, proceed with liver‑first surgery:  
   – Perform non‑anatomic or segmental resections of the four metastases, aiming for R0 margins (>1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous hepatic segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to detect additional lesions.  
   – If major hepatectomy is required, ensure FLR adequacy (≥30 % or >0.5 % body‑weight) and consider PVE pre‑operatively.  
• Post‑hepatectomy recovery (4–6 weeks), then deliver definitive treatment for the rectal primary:  
   – Long‑course chemoradiotherapy (50.4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent capecitabine).  
   – Followed by low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision (protective loop ileostomy as indicated).  
• Adjuvant systemic therapy: resume or complete a total of 8–12 cycles of the same chemotherapy regimen (or switch to a second‑line doublet if progression) to address micrometastatic disease.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and chest CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Precise liver volumetry (future liver remnant percentage).  
• Exact anatomical distribution of the four metastases (unilobar vs bilobar, segmental location).  
• Performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve to gauge surgical fitness.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and portal venous anatomy.  
• Detailed pelvic imaging (MRI) to stage the rectal tumor and assess circumferential resection margin risk.  
• Patient’s preferences regarding sequence of surgery and willingness for combined modality treatment.

Woman, 68 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥10 lesions) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2700 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Massive liver disease with high marker elevation, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer at the abdominal CT scan, three liver metastases (2-3 cm) and confirmed left portal invasion on liver MRI. CEA 310 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Unilateral portal involvement, potentially approachable depending on volume.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the presence of left portal vein invasion raises a critical question about adequate inflow to the left hepatic segments and the size of the future liver remnant (FLR). Without quantitative FLR assessment and a clear plan to secure portal inflow (e.g., portal vein embolization, portal reconstruction, or staged hepatectomy), the case cannot be classified as upfront resectable. The missing FLR volume is a decisive piece of information; therefore the lesion set is deemed potentially resectable pending further evaluation and/or preparatory intervention.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology, obtain disease control, and potentially downsize the liver metastases.  
- Perform baseline liver function tests and high‑resolution CT volumetry (or MRI volumetry) to calculate the FLR after planned resection of the involved segments.  
- If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the portal branches feeding the liver that will be resected (most likely right‑portal embolization if a left‑sided resection is planned, or left‑portal embolization if right‑sided resection is contemplated). Re‑image 2–3 weeks later to confirm hypertrophy.  
- Re‑stage the patient after chemotherapy and PVE:  
   • If all three metastases become amenable to R0 resection with preservation of at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow, proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy.  
   • If portal invasion precludes safe inflow to the left lobe, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: resection of lesions in the future FLR, portal ligation/embolization of the opposite lobe; second stage after hypertrophy).  
   • In selected cases where anatomical constraints remain prohibitive, evaluate adjunctive local therapies (RFA or SBRT) for residual lesions.  
- Primary colon tumor: because it is a left‑sided T3N1 lesion, plan a curative‑intent left‑hemicolectomy. This can be performed either simultaneously with liver resection (if the liver surgery is limited to a minor resection and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits) or in a staged fashion after the liver operation, depending on intra‑operative assessment and patient fitness.  
- After completion of liver and primary resections, administer adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX) to address micrometastatic disease.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA, cross‑sectional imaging, and periodic PET/CT to detect early recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver) after planned resection.  
- Detailed description of the extent of left portal vein invasion (segmental branch vs main trunk) and whether vascular reconstruction is feasible.  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, indocyanine‑green clearance if available).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Molecular profile of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) to refine systemic therapy choice.  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (PET/CT or chest CT) to exclude occult metastases.  
- Planned surgical margins and whether a margin >1 cm is achievable.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, right T3N0M1 colon tumor, single 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII, in close contact with IVC at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 540 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis, major technical question regarding surgical approach.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable  
• Reasoning: The patient has a solitary 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII that abuts the inferior vena cava, making the technical margin challenging. Resection is feasible only if (a) an adequate future liver remnant (≥30 % of total liver volume or >0.5 % body‑weight ratio) can be preserved and (b) vascular control or reconstruction of the IVC can be achieved safely. These determinations require (i) quantitative volumetric imaging of the liver and (ii) a detailed vascular assessment (MRI/CT angiography). Without this information the operation cannot be scheduled outright, but no oncologic contraindication (e.g., widespread extra‑hepatic disease) is present, so the case is not deemed unresectable.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status.  
   – Goal: assess tumor biology, achieve possible downsizing away from the IVC, and lower CEA.  
   – Monitor response with RECIST criteria using contrast‑enhanced MRI (preferred for liver lesions) after every two cycles.  

2. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with vascular phase and 3‑D reconstruction to define residual tumor‑IVC relationship.  
   – Obtain CT‑based volumetry to calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  

3. Decision node based on re‑assessment  
   – If FLR ≥ 30 % and tumor‑IVC distance ≥ 1 cm → proceed to curative liver resection.  
   – If FLR insufficient → schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches, re‑image in 2–4 weeks to confirm hypertrophy; consider two‑stage hepatectomy if needed.  
   – If tumor remains inseparable from IVC → evaluate options: (a) en‑bloc IVC resection with graft reconstruction (high‑risk, reserved for fit patients), (b) extended segmentectomy with intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided margin assessment, or (c) adjunctive local ablative therapy (RFA/SBRT) for residual disease.  

4. Surgical sequencing  
   – Because the primary right‑colon tumor is asymptomatic, adopt a liver‑first approach after chemotherapy, followed by definitive right hemicolectomy 4–6 weeks later (or simultaneous if liver resection is limited to a non‑major segmentectomy and patient fitness permits).  
   – Aim for R0 resection of the liver lesion with negative microscopic margins; intra‑operative ultrasound and possible IVC control/reconstruction should be planned by an experienced hepatobiliary team.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) for 3–6 months, tailored to postoperative recovery and pathology.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for surveillance.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to determine future liver remnant.  
• Detailed vascular imaging (MRI/CT angiography) to define the exact extent of IVC involvement and feasibility of vascular reconstruction.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin) and functional reserve assessment (ICG clearance or LiMAx if available).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve, especially given potential IVC surgery).  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, PET‑CT if indicated).  
• Assessment of tumor biology response after initial chemotherapy (RECIST response, CEA trend).

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 5.6 cm liver metastasis in segment VIII in close contact with the IVC, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although solitary, the central location and caval proximity make a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection technically demanding and potentially unsafe without prior tumor downsizing or vascular planning. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely induction therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of the lesion with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (540 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and hepatic veins.
• If regression occurs or vascular control is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or reconstruction with multidisciplinary discussion with vascular surgery to assess feasibility of tangential IVC resection if needed.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 

E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information

B. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for intensive chemotherapy and for potential major liver surgery.
E. Presence or absence of any extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 69 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma, six liver metastases (1.5-4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 850 ng/mL, BRAF V600E mutation.
MDT Discussion: Unfavorable molecular profile, bilobar liver involvement with systemic potential.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Six bilobar metastases (1.5‑4 cm) are not an absolute technical barrier; resection could be feasible if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume or ≥ 0.5 % body‑weight) can be preserved.  
- The case lacks essential information that directly determines surgical feasibility:  
   • Quantitative FLR assessment (volumetry or CT‑based calculation).  
   • Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelet count, presence of chemotherapy‑induced steato‑hepatitis).  
   • Patient’s performance status and comorbidity burden (ECOG, Charlson index).  
   • Confirmation that there are no extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, nodes).  
- Because these data are missing and because the aggressive BRAF‑V600E biology and very high CEA (850 ng/mL) argue for a “proof‑of‑time” approach, neoadjuvant systemic therapy (or other down‑staging measures) is required before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Baseline work‑up  
   - Full staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis plus liver‑specific MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to confirm number, size, distribution of liver lesions and to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Laboratory panel: liver function tests, coagulation profile, full blood count, CEA trend, LDH.  
   - Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidities; calculate FLR using volumetric software.  

2. Systemic induction therapy (first 3–4 months)  
   - Preferred regimen for BRAF‑mutant mCRC: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (triplet) or a BRAF‑targeted combination (e.g., encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib) if available in a clinical trial or per local protocol.  
   - Aim for at least 4–6 cycles; monitor radiologic response (RECIST) and CEA trend.  

3. Re‑assessment after induction  
   - Repeat liver MRI/CT to evaluate tumor shrinkage, number of viable lesions, and to recalculate FLR.  
   - If FLR is <30 % after anticipated resection, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the future remnant.  

4. Surgical plan  
   - Liver‑first (or staged) approach:  
        • Perform parenchymal‑sparing non‑anatomic or segmental resections to clear all visible metastases while preserving ≥30 % FLR.  
        • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions; treat any residual disease with thermal ablation (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) when resection would compromise liver volume.  
   - After hepatic clearance (R0 resection), address the primary left‑sided colon tumor:  
        • If the primary is still in situ and patient is fit, perform a simultaneous left‑colectomy (laparoscopic or open) if operative time and physiologic reserve allow.  
        • Otherwise, schedule a delayed primary resection 4–6 weeks after liver surgery, once recovery is adequate.  

5. Adjuvant/Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Continue the same systemic regimen (or switch to a maintenance protocol) for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy, aiming to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
   - Consider enrolment in a BRAF‑targeted clinical trial (e.g., BEACON‑CRC) if postoperative recovery permits.  

6. Post‑operative surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- ECOG performance status / detailed comorbidity index (Charlson).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelet count).  
- Precise volumetric measurement of future liver remnant.  
- Confirmation of absence (or presence) of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, nodal disease).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. still in situ, surgical margins, T/N stage).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status (to confirm exclusivity with BRAF).  
- Details of prior or planned systemic therapy (agents, cycles).  

These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 65 years old, T4N1M1 rectal tumor, four liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Immuno-sensitive profile, discussion on optimal therapeutic sequence.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of four liver metastases does not automatically preclude resection, but critical technical information is lacking. Definitive assessment requires (a) high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) with segmental mapping to determine size, bilobar distribution and proximity to major vessels, and (b) volumetric calculation of the future liver remnant (FLR) to confirm that ≥30 % of functional liver will remain (or FLR/weight > 0.5 %). Without these data we cannot confirm that an R0 resection with adequate hepatic reserve is feasible, thus the case remains potentially resectable pending further imaging and volumetric analysis.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic therapy tailored to the MSI‑high, RAS‑wild‑type profile: first‑line pembrolizumab (immune checkpoint inhibitor) ± fluoropyrimidine‑based chemotherapy as per current ESMO/ASCO guidance for MSI‑H metastatic colorectal cancer.  
- Concurrently schedule short‑course (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the T4 rectal primary, depending on sphincter‑preservation goals and anticipated timing of hepatic surgery.  
- Perform restaging after 2–3 months of systemic therapy (MRI liver, CT chest/abdomen, pelvic MRI) to evaluate response of hepatic lesions and rectal tumor.  
- If hepatic disease shows stable disease or partial response and FLR assessment confirms adequacy, proceed with a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   • Stage‑1: anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (potentially two‑stage or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS – if FLR insufficient) aiming for R0 resection of all four metastases.  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance; consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  
- After hepatic resection and recovery (≈6‑8 weeks), complete definitive rectal management:  
   • If short‑course radiotherapy was given, proceed to low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision (TME) and protective ileostomy.  
   • If long‑course chemoradiotherapy was administered, schedule surgery 8‑12 weeks post‑radiation.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of immunotherapy ± chemotherapy) for 6 months, guided by pathological response and residual disease.  
- Ongoing surveillance with 3‑month imaging (CT/MRI) for the first 2 years, then 6‑month intervals, plus serial CEA.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed liver imaging (MRI with liver‑specific contrast or high‑resolution multiphase CT) showing exact size, number, segmental location and relationship to vascular structures.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (FLR) and liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelet count).  
- Performance status/ECOG and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve, ASA score).  
- Exact distance of rectal tumor from anal verge and involvement of adjacent organs (prostate, sacrum) to plan surgical margins and need for exenteration.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung nodules, peritoneal implants) on chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- BRAF mutation status (if not already known) and baseline tumor mutational burden.  
- Baseline laboratory values (CBC, liver panel, renal function, coagulation).

The patient presents with four liver metastases in the setting of a T4N1 rectal tumor. Although the liver disease may be technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection, the MSI-H profile indicates a high likelihood of major response to immunotherapy. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is potentially resectable, but surgery is not the first step given the expected efficacy of systemic immunotherapy.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 4 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.a chest CT scan

B. First-line systemic immunotherapy (mandatory)
• Initiate immunotherapy according to MDT decision as first-line treatment for MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer.
• The objective is major tumor regression and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical re-evaluation after response
• If a major radiologic response occurs, reassess segmental resectability.
• Plan biopsy of the primary rectal tumor and liver metastases to assess tumor response to immunotherapy
• Consider parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided liver resections only if residual lesions persist and complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic immunotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals

Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1300 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: contact with right hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular invasion, significant operative risk.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has eight bilobar metastases with contact to the right hepatic vein and superior vascular invasion, making an R0 resection impossible without modification of disease burden or liver remnant augmentation. Current imaging does not demonstrate that a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 %/kg body weight) can be preserved, and the vascular involvement precludes a single‑stage hepatectomy. Therefore resection is contingent on (a) systemic down‑staging chemotherapy to assess tumor biology and reduce lesion size/number, and (b) a hypertrophy strategy (portal vein embolisation or two‑stage hepatectomy) to obtain an adequate FLR. Until these prerequisites are fulfilled the disease must be classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
- Re‑image (triphasic CT + gadoxetic‑enhanced MRI) after 2–3 months to evaluate RECIST response, lesion shrinkage, and to quantify FLR volume.  
- If disease is stable or responding and no new extra‑hepatic sites appear:  
   • Plan a liver‑first, staged approach.  
   • First stage: resect left‑lateral or segment 3 lesions (or ablate lesions unsuitable for resection) and perform right portal vein embolisation to induce left‑lobe hypertrophy.  
   • Wait 4–6 weeks, repeat volumetry; aim for FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥0.5 %/kg).  
   • Second stage: right hepatectomy (including resection of right hepatic vein if oncologically necessary and technically feasible) to clear remaining disease.  
   • Consider intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided radiofrequency ablation for lesions adherent to the right hepatic vein that cannot be safely dissected.  
- After completion of hepatic clearance and patient recovery, proceed to definitive resection of the primary right‑colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) – either simultaneous with the first liver stage if the patient’s operative risk is acceptable, or as a separate procedure after hepatic surgery (liver‑first strategy).  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or adapted based on response) for at least 6 months.  
- If imaging after initial chemotherapy shows progression (new lesions, growth of >3 lesions, or loss of resectability), continue systemic therapy and consider palliative options (e.g., Y‑90 radio‑embolisation, systemic therapy, or best‑supportive care).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current performance status (ECOG/ASA) and detailed cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Baseline liver function tests and assessment of underlying liver quality (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Precise volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
- Extent of right hepatic vein involvement (encasement vs. abutment) and whether hepatic arterial/portal inflow to the right lobe can be preserved.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, distant lymph nodes) on chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Symptoms or obstruction from the primary colon tumor (bleeding, perforation).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases with MRI showing contact with the right hepatic vein, in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (1300 ng/mL). The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and venous contact make a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate venous outflow and future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.
 
Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 4 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1300 ng/mL) and the BRAF V600E mutation, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
 
B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab;
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.
 
C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response and reassess the relationship to the right hepatic vein.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.
 
D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic response occurs with regression of venous contact and significant reduction in tumor burden allowing parenchymal-sparing resections with preserved venous drainage.
 
E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy..
 
F. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic immunotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals 
 
Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise segmental distribution of the 8 lesions within the left and the right liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
B. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
C. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
