Case_Content:
Woman, 55 years old, left colon cancer, multiple bilobar metastases at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 2100 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 amplified.
MDT Discussion: Particular molecular profile, possible sensitivity to an anti-HER2 approach.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases, but critical information needed to determine technical feasibility is absent. Specifically, the number and maximal size of lesions, their relationship to major vascular structures, the calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease are not provided. Without these data a definitive judgment of upfront resectability cannot be made, so the case must be considered potentially resectable pending further assessment.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic therapy aimed at tumor down‑staging and at exploiting the HER2 amplification: a HER2‑directed doublet (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab‑deruxtecan) combined with a standard chemotherapy backbone (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).  
- Monitor tumor markers (CEA) and radiologic response after 2–3 months (or after 4–6 cycles) with high‑resolution liver MRI and CT.  
- Re‑assess resectability after systemic therapy: calculate FLR, map residual disease, and determine whether an R0 resection of all hepatic lesions is achievable.  
- If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, plan pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
- Decide sequencing of primary‑tumor and liver surgery based on symptomatology and response:  
   • If the primary colon lesion is asymptomatic, adopt a liver‑first approach after systemic therapy response.  
   • If the primary becomes symptomatic or obstructive, perform a diverting or resective colorectal surgery first, then proceed to liver surgery.  
- Aim for an R0 hepatic resection (or combined resection + thermal ablation/SBRT for lesions in unfavorable locations) while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
- Post‑operative management: adjuvant systemic therapy (continue HER2‑targeted regimen) for 3–6 months, with surveillance imaging and CEA monitoring every 3–4 months for the first two years.  
- Consider enrollment in a clinical trial of HER2‑targeted therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer if available.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Performance status (ECOG) and comorbidity burden (Charlson index).  
- Detailed liver imaging: exact number of metastases, maximal diameter of each lesion, proximity to major vessels/ biliary structures.  
- Quantitative assessment of future liver remnant volume (CT volumetry or MRI).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status (to confirm suitability of anti‑HER2 regimen).  
- Microsatellite instability / mismatch repair status.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelet count) and any evidence of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury.  
- Patient’s nutritional status and any need for pre‑habilitation.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability assessment and to tailor the neoadjuvant regimen and surgical plan.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The hepatic lesions are centrally located and are in contact with the inferior vena cava and the right hepatic vein, which makes an R0 resection technically demanding and may require vascular reconstruction. Whether a curative‑intent hepatectomy can be performed safely depends on (a) the ability to achieve negative margins after possible tumor shrinkage and (b) the volume and functional capacity of the future liver remnant (FLR). Both of these points require further pre‑operative actions (systemic down‑staging chemotherapy, volumetric imaging, and possibly portal vein embolisation) before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX‑IRI ± bevacizumab) as conversion therapy to assess tumor biology and to attempt downsizing of the central liver metastases.  
• Simultaneously start neoadjuvant radiotherapy for the upper rectal primary (short‑course 5 Gy × 5 days or long‑course chemoradiation) because the primary is T3N1 and will require TME.  
• After 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles) perform restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) and repeat triphasic CT to:  
    – Measure the residual size of each metastasis and reassess vascular contact;  
    – Calculate FLR volume (target ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % if steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated injury).  
• If the lesions have responded sufficiently and FLR is adequate:  
    – Adopt a liver‑first (reverse) approach: perform hepatic resection first, using either (i) extended right hepatectomy with reconstruction of the right hepatic vein/IVC (patch graft or interposition graft) or (ii) central hepatectomy preserving left lateral segments (II‑III) if oncologically safe.  
    – If FLR is borderline, perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) 2–3 weeks before liver resection to induce hypertrophy of the left lateral segments.  
    – Consider intra‑operative ultrasound and, if needed, adjunctive local ablative techniques (RFA/MWA) for lesions that cannot be safely resected.  
• After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈ 6–8 weeks), proceed to definitive rectal surgery (low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision) following the interval radiotherapy.  
• Complete the treatment course with adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (additional 4–6 cycles) and regular surveillance (CEA, cross‑sectional imaging every 3–6 months).  
• If after conversion therapy the vascular involvement persists or FLR remains insufficient, discuss a two‑stage hepatectomy (or ALPPS) versus definitive non‑surgical management.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Exact number of liver metastases and their segmental distribution.  
• Quantitative FLR measurement (volumetry) and baseline liver function (bilirubin, ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh).  
• Extent of IVC/right hepatic vein invasion (partial contact vs encasement, length of involvement).  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
• Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve (relevant for major vascular reconstruction).  
• Molecular profile of the primary (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI) to guide targeted agents in the chemotherapy regimen.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with centrally located liver metastases (3–5 cm) in contact with the IVC and the right hepatic vein in the setting of an upper rectal T3N1 tumor, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is not specified as excessive, the venous involvement makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unsafe without complex vascular control or reconstruction. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert HPB / vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvis MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (580 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and reduction of venous contact.

C. Expert vascular restaging
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the IVC and right hepatic vein.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with complex surgery to assess feasibility of venous reconstruction if required or right hepatomy including en-bloc resection of the right hepatic vein according to the future liver remnant.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If regression occurs or venous reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC and/or hepatic vein reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Surgical management after restaging : management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning 
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

F. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise extent and depth of contact with the IVC and right hepatic vein on MRI.
B. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, and circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI influencing surgical approach and anastomotic risk
C. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Trend and quantification of circulating tumor cells over time.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan and normal CEA at 3 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Biological discordance, question regarding the utility of CEA follow-up in this profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The case lacks essential anatomic information required to determine whether a margin‑negative (R0) hepatectomy can be performed while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR). Specifically, a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or high‑quality multiphase CT) with volumetric analysis, and a detailed description of the number, size, and bilobar distribution of the metastases are missing. Without these data, a definitive “Resectable upfront” decision cannot be made, but there is no documented extra‑hepatic disease or contraindicating comorbidity that would render the disease unresectable. Therefore the patient is classified as potentially resectable, pending completion of the missing imaging/volumetric assessment (or, alternatively, neoadjuvant systemic therapy to downsize disease if the lesions are borderline).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline work‑up  
   - Obtain a liver‑specific MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) with 3‑D volumetry to define tumor burden, FLR, and vascular involvement.  
   - Complete staging PET‑CT or high‑quality chest CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
   - Record performance status (ECOG), comorbidities (Charlson index), liver function tests, and baseline CA 19‑9.  

2. Multidisciplinary treatment planning  
   - If imaging confirms that an R0 resection is technically feasible with an FLR ≥ 30 % (in a normal liver) or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury, proceed to upfront combined resection (simultaneous right hemicolectomy and hepatectomy) provided the patient is fit (ECOG 0‑1, adequate cardiopulmonary reserve).  
   - If FLR is insufficient or disease is borderline (e.g., >3 lesions, bilobar disease, large tumor burden), initiate neoadjuvant systemic therapy:  
     • Preferred regimen: FOLFOX or FOLFIRI + anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) for KRAS‑mutated disease.  
     • Consider adding a second biologic (e.g., anti‑EGFR) only if KRAS wild‑type; in this case KRAS is mutant, so anti‑VEGF is appropriate.  
   - Re‑image after 2–3 months (or after 6 cycles) to assess response and re‑calculate FLR.  

3. Conversion/Down‑staging  
   - If tumor burden decreases to allow R0 resection with adequate FLR, plan either:  
     a) Staged approach – primary right‑sided colon resection first, followed by liver resection after recovery (2–4 weeks).  
     b) Liver‑first (reverse) approach – portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR remains borderline, then hepatic resection, and finally colon resection. Choice depends on symptomatology of the primary tumor and relative disease burden.  

4. Surgical strategy  
   - Aim for R0 margins (≥1 cm when feasible, otherwise >5 mm).  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate all lesions; consider adjunctive thermal ablation (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy for lesions in locations that would otherwise preclude safe resection.  
   - Preserve at least 30 % functional liver parenchyma; if needed, perform right or extended right hepatectomy with left lateral segment preservation, or a parenchymal‑sparing (segmental/segmentectomy) approach.  

5. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   - After complete resection, resume systemic chemotherapy (same regimen or switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for 3–6 months to address micrometastatic disease, given high risk (T4, N2, KRAS‑mutated, synchronous disease).  

6. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA (despite current low level) every 3 months, liver MRI every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Monitor for recurrence; consider repeat local therapy (ablation, repeat hepatectomy) if isolated hepatic recurrence occurs.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics: number of metastases, maximal diameter of each, unilateral vs. bilateral (bilobar) distribution.  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) and liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT).  
- Performance status (ECOG), comorbidity burden (Charlson index), cardiopulmonary assessment.  
- Baseline CA 19‑9 level (useful prognostic marker).  
- Confirmation of absence or presence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes) via PET‑CT or dedicated chest imaging.  
- Results of pre‑operative liver function tests and any prior chemotherapy‑related liver injury.  

These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer, bilobar metastases (1.5-3 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 400 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, POLE mutation detected.
MDT Discussion: Hypermutated profile, rare, may justify immunotherapy in some strategies.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has synchronous, bilobar liver metastases that are small (1.5‑3 cm) and therefore technically amenable to resection. However, the case description lacks critical information required to confirm that an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) and vascular inflow/outflow. A pre‑operative liver volumetric study (CT‑ or MRI‑based) and a detailed mapping of lesion location relative to major hepatic vessels are needed. If the FLR is insufficient, portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy would be required before definitive surgery, making the current status “potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initial work‑up  
   – Obtain high‑quality multiphase liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast to define number, segmental distribution, and vascular proximity of all metastases.  
   – Perform CT‑ or MRI‑based volumetry to calculate FLR; plan PVE if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in steatotic liver).  
   – Complete staging for extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET‑CT) and assess performance status (ECOG), comorbidities (Charlson), and liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).

   – Because the disease is synchronous, CEA is markedly elevated (400 ng/mL) and the primary is left‑sided, start a doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) – RAS wild‑type predicts benefit.  
   – Given the POLE hyper‑mutated phenotype, add a PD‑1 inhibitor (e.g., pembrolizumab) in a clinical‑trial setting or off‑label if no trial is available, as hypermutated tumors can respond to checkpoint blockade.  
   – Treat for 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles), reassess radiologically and with tumor markers (CEA).  

• Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI and volumetry.  
   – If all lesions have responded or remained stable and an R0 resection is technically feasible with adequate FLR, proceed to definitive liver surgery.  

• Surgical sequence (liver‑first preferred)  
   – If FLR is sufficient, perform a single‑stage, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy (anatomical or non‑anatomic) to clear all hepatic disease; use intra‑operative ultrasound to guide resection and consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  
   – If FLR is inadequate, perform PVE now (if not done earlier) and schedule a second‑stage hepatectomy after hypertrophy (typically 4–6 weeks).  
   – After hepatic clearance, address the primary colon tumor with a left hemicolectomy; this can be done simultaneously if the liver operation is limited and the patient’s physiologic reserve allows, otherwise stage it 4–6 weeks later.  

• Post‑operative/adjuvant therapy  
   – Continue systemic therapy to complete a total of 6 months (including the neoadjuvant portion).  
   – Maintain PD‑1 inhibitor for the duration of the adjuvant period if the patient tolerated it and no progression occurred.  
   – Follow with surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
Essential information not provided that is required for a definitive plan:  
- Detailed hepatic imaging (MRI with segmental mapping) showing exact number of metastases, their relationship to major vessels, and whether any lesions are unresectable due to location.  
- Quantitative liver volumetry to determine future liver remnant volume.  
- Assessment of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, lymph nodes).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidity burden (Charlson index), and baseline liver function tests.  
- Cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., VO₂ max, cardiac evaluation) to gauge tolerance of major hepatectomy.  

These data are needed to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive “resectable upfront” or to decide on alternative non‑surgical strategies.

   – Start a doublet oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., mFOLFOX6) combined with bevacizumab, because the tumor harbors an NRAS mutation and is EGFR‑resistant.

• Restaging work‑up (after 3–6 cycles)  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or triphasic CT) with volumetric analysis to calculate future liver remnant (FLR).

   – If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % with adequate function) and all lesions are amenable to R0 resection, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery.

   – If disease remains extensive or progresses, continue systemic therapy or consider locoregional options (RFA, SBRT) and discuss palliative intent.  
• Surgical plan (when resectability confirmed)  
   – Aim for anatomic or non‑anatomic resections that achieve negative margins (≥ 1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   – Coordinate resection of the primary transverse colon tumor: either simultaneous colon and liver resection (if patient fitness permits) or staged resection (colon first, followed by liver surgery after recovery).  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any additional lesions.  
   – Pathologic assessment of margins and nodal status.  
• Post‑operative management  
   – Resume the same systemic regimen (or switch to FOLFIRI if oxaliplatin‑related neuropathy develops) for 6 months as adjuvant therapy, provided postoperative recovery is adequate.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring every 3 months and imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for surveillance.  
   – Consider enrollment in a clinical trial targeting NRAS‑mutated mCRC if available.

Essential information not provided that is needed for a definitive plan:

Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The three liver metastases include invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, which makes a standard hepatectomy technically demanding and may require vascular reconstruction. The case notes that “volume to be assessed,” indicating that the future liver remnant (FLR) has not been quantified. Adequate FLR (≥30 % of total liver volume or >0.5 % body weight) is a decisive technical criterion for safe resection. Because this critical information is missing, and because the vascular involvement may necessitate adjunctive measures (e.g., portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy, or ALPPS), the lesion set cannot be declared resectable upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy: preferred regimen FOLFOXIRI + anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS‑wild type status, aiming for maximal tumor shrinkage and “biological proof of time.”  
• Re‑image after 2–3 months (contrast‑enhanced MRI and CT) to assess:  
   – Response of hepatic lesions (size reduction, especially at the hepatic vein confluence)  
   – Presence of new extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes)  
   – Calculate FLR volume using volumetric software.  
• If FLR < 30 % or borderline, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segment(s) to be resected, with repeat volumetry 2–3 weeks later.  
• If vascular invasion persists but tumor burden is reduced and FLR is adequate, plan a liver‑first operation:  
   – Extended right or left hepatectomy (depending on lesion distribution) with en‑bloc resection of the involved hepatic vein confluence and reconstruction using a cryopreserved venous graft or prosthetic conduit.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm negative margins (R0) and preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow.  
• After hepatic resection and recovery (≈4–6 weeks), perform definitive resection of the primary left‑colon tumor (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy). If the primary tumor is symptomatic or obstructing, consider simultaneous resection only if operative time and physiologic stress are acceptable.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 3–6 cycles of the same regimen) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
• Enroll patient in a strict surveillance program (CEA, cross‑sectional imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Precise volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant (FLR).  
• Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, indocyanine‑green clearance) to gauge hepatic reserve.  
• Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve, ASA classification).  
• Exact size of each metastasis and their segmental distribution (unilateral vs. bilobar).  
• Confirmation of absence or presence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung nodules, peritoneal implants) on chest CT or PET‑CT.  
• Staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, nodal status) and any symptoms requiring urgent colorectal surgery.  
• Details of hepatic vein involvement (which branches, length of invasion) to plan reconstruction.

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: Four bilobar metastases measuring 3‑5 cm are technically resectable only if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) can be preserved. The case description does not provide FLR volume, segmental distribution of the lesions, liver function tests, or performance status, all of which are decisive for determining whether a single‑stage resection, a two‑stage approach, portal vein embolisation or ALPPS is required. Consequently, resection cannot be performed upfront and must await further anatomical and functional assessment, as well as consideration of neoadjuvant systemic therapy to address the unfavorable biology (high CEA, synchronous disease, BRAF D594G mutation).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic therapy aimed at tumor down‑staging and biological selection: preferred regimen is a triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab; consider adding a BRAF‑directed agent (e.g., encorafenib + cetuximab) if later trials or institutional protocols support use in non‑V600E BRAF mutants.  
• Re‑image after 3–4 cycles (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) to assess radiologic response, calculate FLR, and re‑evaluate resectability.  
• If FLR is adequate (≥30 % without portal hypertension) and disease remains resectable, proceed with a liver‑first strategy:  
 – Perform portal vein embolisation (PVE) if FLR is borderline (20‑30 %).  
 – Schedule either a single‑stage extended hepatectomy (e.g., right hepatectomy + segmental left‑lobe resections) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (right‑sided resection first, then left‑sided completion after hypertrophy).  
 – Aim for R0 margins (>1 mm) and preserve at least 30 % functional liver parenchyma.  
• After successful liver resection, address the primary right‑sided colon tumor: if the primary is asymptomatic, a simultaneous right hemicolectomy can be performed; if intra‑operative complexity or patient condition dictates, defer primary resection to a second operation within 4–6 weeks.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) should be given, tailored to the response achieved and tolerability.  
• Enroll the patient in a clinical trial if available (e.g., BRAF‑targeted therapy in the peri‑operative setting).  
• Follow‑up with serial CEA, imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• ECOG performance status / ASA classification  
• Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury  
• Detailed segmental location of each liver metastasis and volumetric analysis to calculate future liver remnant  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) beyond what is stated  
• KRAS mutation status and microsatellite instability / dMMR status (relevant for systemic therapy choice)  
• Comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary) that may affect surgical fitness  
• Planned or prior neoadjuvant therapy (if any) and response assessment.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Six metastases 2–4 cm each are technically resectable only if a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % can be preserved; the current CT does not provide volumetric data to confirm this.  
- The disease is synchronous, T4 N2, with very high CEA (320 ng/mL) and circulating tumor cells, indicating aggressive biology that traditionally prompts “proof of time” with neoadjuvant chemotherapy before committing to surgery.  
- Therefore a prerequisite systemic therapy (and/or volumetric liver assessment) is required before an R0 liver resection can be planned.

1. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start a 3‑month intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status and high‑risk primary.

   - Primary colon tumor: perform oncologic left‑sided colectomy with en‑bloc resection of the T4 lesion (primary first) followed by recovery, unless the patient’s condition permits a simultaneous liver‑first approach.

     • For lesions in difficult locations, supplement resection with intra‑operative thermal ablation (RFA/SBRT) to achieve complete eradication.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic therapy for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment, tailoring biologic agents to RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   - Serial CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, to detect recurrence early.
